The Mail Room/Lesson 29/Lesson text (draft)

Multiclass Learnability

Lesson text (draft) · Teacher's sheet

Three hundred folders and one hungry folder

The auditor signed, and the product team got its new plan. The filter no longer answers junk or keep: it files every message into one of 300 folders, invoices, newsletters, travel, receipts, one for each team’s project, and junk. The learner behind it is lesson 17a’s four-folder filter grown up, a linear multiclass predictor with one weight vector per folder, trained by ERM on messages described by 30 features. It works. And then the launch review asks the question every launch since lesson 2 has had to answer: how many labelled messages does this need, and how sure can you be?

You reach for the fundamental theorem that lesson 28 has just finished proving: the labels a class needs grow with its VC dimension. But open the definition of the VC dimension and look at what it measures: how many points a class can label in every possible way with two labels. Junk or keep. Shattering asks for all 2∣C∣2^{|C|}2∣C∣ yes/no labellings of a set CCC of ∣C∣|C|∣C∣ messages. Your hypotheses don’t answer yes or no; they answer “folder 17” or “folder 243”. The VC dimension simply isn’t defined for them, and the review is stuck.

There is a second, stranger problem. Last week the team shipped auto-folders: a user can gather a group of senders, and all their mail goes into a folder named after that group. Mail from everyone else stays in the inbox. Right now no user has made a folder, so the true rule is “everything stays in the inbox”. The learner is ERM over all possible auto-folder rules, and its training error is zero. Yet users are furious: mail from people they have never written to before is vanishing into a mysterious folder.

Here is what happened. All 60 labelled messages said “inbox”, and many rules fit that. The team’s ERM picked the one that makes a folder out of every sender it has not seen. It is consistent: every labelled message really did come from a sender it has seen, and those stay in the inbox. On fresh mail it is a disaster. In the simulation below, 90% of the company’s mail comes from one sender (the all-staff announcements) and the rest is spread over 999 other senders:

import random

rng, n, m = random.Random(0), 1000, 60
p = [0.9] + [0.1 / (n - 1)] * (n - 1)
senders = rng.choices(range(n), weights=p, k=m)
seen = set(senders)
L_bad = sum(p[x] for x in range(n) if x not in seen)
L_good = 0.0
print(len(seen), round(L_bad, 4), L_good)

It prints 9 0.0992 0.0. The 60 labels came from only 9 distinct senders, so the team’s rule hides the mail of the other 991, about 9.9% of all mail, while the rule “everything in the inbox”, which is just as consistent, is perfect. Both are ERM. One learns, one doesn’t.

So you have two bugs. You cannot say how many labels a 300-folder rule needs, because the tool you would use only speaks in two labels. And you have an ERM over a class of folder rules that learns badly, even though lesson 6a promised that, for two labels, every ERM learns whenever anything does. This lesson fixes both.

What carries over from two labels

Let’s set the stage with the words we already have. A multiclass problem is one where each label is one of kkk values. We write the label set as [k]={1,2,…,k}[k] = \{1, 2, \dots, k\}[k]={1,2,…,k}, the numbers from 1 to kkk, so with 300 folders a label is a number from 1 to 300. A hypothesis is still a function hhh from the domain X\mathcal XX (all possible messages) to the labels, now written h:X→[k]h: \mathcal X \to [k]h:X→[k], and a hypothesis class H\mathcal HH is a set of them. We write [k]X[k]^{\mathcal X}[k]X for the set of all functions from X\mathcal XX to [k][k][k], so “H⊆[k]X\mathcal H \subseteq [k]^{\mathcal X}H⊆[k]X” just says that every member of H\mathcal HH is such a function.

The loss is the 0-1 loss of lesson 3: a hypothesis pays 1 for a wrong folder and 0 for the right one, whichever wrong folder it picks. So the empirical risk LS(h)L_S(h)LS​(h) is still the fraction of the training sequence SSS that hhh files wrongly, and the true risk LD(h)L_{\mathcal D}(h)LD​(h) is the chance that it files the next message wrongly, when messages and their folders are drawn from the distribution D\mathcal DD. Recall also from lesson 2 that ERM (empirical risk minimization) is any learner that returns a hypothesis in H\mathcal HH with the smallest empirical risk, and that when several hypotheses tie, which one it returns is up to the particular ERM. That freedom will matter a great deal at the end of this lesson.

The definitions of lesson 3 carry over word for word, because they never mentioned how many labels there are. A class is PAC learnable when some learner, given m≥mH(ε,δ)m \ge m_{\mathcal H}(\varepsilon, \delta)m≥mH​(ε,δ) i.i.d. examples labelled by some hypothesis in the class (the realizable case), returns a hypothesis with true risk at most ε\varepsilonε with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ. Here ε\varepsilonε is the accuracy you tolerate, δ\deltaδ the chance of failure you tolerate, mmm the number of examples, and mHm_{\mathcal H}mH​ the sample complexity, the smallest number of examples that suffices. It is agnostic PAC learnable when, with no assumption that any hypothesis is perfect, some learner gets within ε\varepsilonε of the best hypothesis in the class. And it has the uniform convergence property (lesson 4) when enough examples make every hypothesis’s empirical risk close to its true risk at once; lesson 4 showed that this makes every ERM a successful learner.

What does not carry over is the yardstick. Lesson 6a measured a class by its restriction to a finite set C={c1,…,cr}C = \{c_1, \dots, c_r\}C={c1​,…,cr​}, the set of label vectors the class produces there,

HC={(h(c1),…,h(cr)):h∈H},\mathcal H_C = \{ (h(c_1), \dots, h(c_r)) : h \in \mathcal H \},HC​={(h(c1​),…,h(cr​)):h∈H},

which now lives inside [k]r[k]^r[k]r, the vectors of rrr folder numbers. Read it as before: one vector of answers per hypothesis, collected in braces, duplicates kept once. If two hypotheses file two messages as (1, 2) and a third as (1, 3), then HC={(1,2),(1,3)}\mathcal H_C = \{(1, 2), (1, 3)\}HC​={(1,2),(1,3)}; the first snippet of the next section computes one. For two labels, H\mathcal HH shatters CCC when HC\mathcal H_CHC​ contains all 2r2^r2r vectors, and the VC dimension is the size of the largest shattered set.

Lesson 6a stated the fundamental theorem of statistical learning, and lesson 28 proved it with explicit constants. For two labels, a class with VC dimension ddd is learnable exactly when ddd is finite, and any ERM learns it. With noisy labels, no learner can do with fewer than (d+log⁡(1/δ))/(1024 ε2)(d + \log(1/\delta))/(1024\,\varepsilon^2)(d+log(1/δ))/(1024ε2) labels (for ε≤1/(82)\varepsilon \le 1/(8\sqrt2)ε≤1/(82​) and δ≤1/8\delta \le 1/8δ≤1/8), and ERM succeeds with order (dlog⁡(1/ε)+log⁡(1/δ))/ε2(d\log(1/\varepsilon) + \log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon^2(dlog(1/ε)+log(1/δ))/ε2, the theorem’s ceiling up to that extra log⁡(1/ε)\log(1/\varepsilon)log(1/ε). With clean labels, ERM succeeds with order (dlog⁡(1/ε)+log⁡(1/δ))/ε(d\log(1/\varepsilon) + \log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon(dlog(1/ε)+log(1/δ))/ε. The engine of the ceilings was Sauer’s lemma: a class of VC dimension ddd produces at most ∑i=0d(ri)\sum_{i=0}^{d}\binom{r}{i}∑i=0d​(ir​) labellings on rrr points, at most (er/d)d(er/d)^d(er/d)d once r≥dr \ge dr≥d, a polynomial in rrr rather than 2r2^r2r.

So the question is: what should “shatter” mean when there are 300 labels?

Two choices per message

Let’s work it out on a class small enough to hold in your head. Suppose the scoring service from lesson 6a now returns an urgency score between 0 and 1, and the filter files each message into one of k=3k = 3k=3 urgency folders: 1 (low), 2 (normal), 3 (urgent). A rule picks two cut points, t1≤t2t_1 \le t_2t1​≤t2​, and files a message as low if its score is at most t1t_1t1​, normal if it is above t1t_1t1​ but at most t2t_2t2​, and urgent if it is above t2t_2t2​. Call these rules urgency levels. With cut points 0.5 and 1.0, a message scoring 0.3 is low and one scoring 0.7 is normal.

Now take two messages, scoring 0.3 and 0.7. A first idea would be to ask for all 32=93^2 = 932=9 ways to file them, by analogy with 222^222. But urgency levels can never file 0.3 as urgent and 0.7 as low, because a higher score never gets a lower folder. Asking for all k∣C∣k^{|C|}k∣C∣ labellings is so demanding that hardly any interesting class would shatter anything, and the measure would say nothing.

Here is a gentler question, and it is the right one. For each message, you pick two candidate folders. Then ask: can the class produce every mixture, every way of choosing one of the two candidates for each message? For 0.3, pick low or normal; for 0.7, pick normal or urgent. That is four mixtures, the two-label question in disguise: on each message there is a binary choice, “first candidate or second”. Here are the four, tried against urgency levels (in the code, a 1 in B means that message takes its first candidate):

from itertools import product

k, C = 3, [0.3, 0.7]
f0, f1 = (1, 2), (2, 3)

def levels(t):
    return lambda x: 1 + sum(x > tj for tj in t)

cuts = [0.0, 0.5, 1.0]
H = [levels(t) for t in product(cuts, repeat=k - 1)
     if list(t) == sorted(t)]
H_C = {tuple(h(c) for c in C) for h in H}
for B in product([0, 1], repeat=len(C)):
    mix = tuple(f0[i] if B[i] else f1[i] for i in range(len(C)))
    print(B, mix, mix in H_C)

It prints

(0, 0) (2, 3) True
(0, 1) (2, 2) True
(1, 0) (1, 3) True
(1, 1) (1, 2) True

All four mixtures are achieved. In the new sense, urgency levels shatter the two messages. Notice that the choice of candidates was part of the work: had we offered “low or urgent” for 0.7, the mixture “normal, low” would have been demanded, and no urgency level files a higher score lower.

[diagram:two-choices: built on the lesson page]

What about three messages? Try scores 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8 with any candidates you like, and you will always find a mixture the class cannot produce. Here is why, in one line of reasoning. Call the two candidates of message iii its lower one, loi\mathrm{lo}_iloi​, and its upper one, hii\mathrm{hi}_ihii​, so loi<hii\mathrm{lo}_i < \mathrm{hi}_iloi​<hii​. The mixture that takes the upper candidate for message 1 and the lower one for message 2 must be achievable, and urgency levels never file a higher score lower, so hi1≤lo2\mathrm{hi}_1 \le \mathrm{lo}_2hi1​≤lo2​. The same goes for messages 2 and 3. So lo1<hi1≤lo2<hi2≤lo3<hi3\mathrm{lo}_1 < \mathrm{hi}_1 \le \mathrm{lo}_2 < \mathrm{hi}_2 \le \mathrm{lo}_3 < \mathrm{hi}_3lo1​<hi1​≤lo2​<hi2​≤lo3​<hi3​, a chain with three strict steps up from lo1≥1\mathrm{lo}_1 \ge 1lo1​≥1, which forces hi3≥4\mathrm{hi}_3 \ge 4hi3​≥4. There is no folder 4. With three folders, two messages is the most this class can shatter.

The Natarajan dimension

Now let’s write the idea down precisely. Each message xxx of the set CCC gets two candidate folders, which we collect into two functions: f0(x)f_0(x)f0​(x), the first candidate, and f1(x)f_1(x)f1​(x), the second. A mixture is described by the set BBB of messages that take their first candidate; the rest take their second.

Definition (shattering, multiclass). A finite set C⊆XC \subseteq \mathcal XC⊆X is shattered by a class H⊆[k]X\mathcal H \subseteq [k]^{\mathcal X}H⊆[k]X if there exist two functions f0,f1:C→[k]f_0, f_1: C \to [k]f0​,f1​:C→[k] such that f0(x)≠f1(x)f_0(x) \ne f_1(x)f0​(x)=f1​(x) for every x∈Cx \in Cx∈C, and for every subset B⊆CB \subseteq CB⊆C there is a hypothesis h∈Hh \in \mathcal Hh∈H with

h(x)=f0(x) for all x∈Bandh(x)=f1(x) for all x∈C∖B.h(x) = f_0(x) \text{ for all } x \in B \quad \text{and} \quad h(x) = f_1(x) \text{ for all } x \in C \setminus B.h(x)=f0​(x) for all x∈Bandh(x)=f1​(x) for all x∈C∖B.

Read it piece by piece.

  • f0,f1:C→[k]f_0, f_1: C \to [k]f0​,f1​:C→[k] are the two lists of candidates: each assigns a folder to every message of CCC. The condition f0(x)≠f1(x)f_0(x) \ne f_1(x)f0​(x)=f1​(x) says the two candidates for a message are genuinely different folders.
  • B⊆CB \subseteq CB⊆C is any subset of CCC, including the empty set and CCC itself; there are 2∣C∣2^{|C|}2∣C∣ of them, one per mixture.
  • C∖BC \setminus BC∖B (“CCC minus BBB”) is the set of messages of CCC that are not in BBB.
  • The display asks for one hypothesis hhh that gives the first candidate on every message of BBB and the second candidate on every other message of CCC.

In plain words: H\mathcal HH shatters CCC when you can pick two different candidate folders for each message of CCC so that the class achieves every way of choosing between them. In our example, C={0.3,0.7}C = \{0.3, 0.7\}C={0.3,0.7}, f0=(low,normal)f_0 = (\text{low}, \text{normal})f0​=(low,normal), f1=(normal,urgent)f_1 = (\text{normal}, \text{urgent})f1​=(normal,urgent), and B={0.3}B = \{0.3\}B={0.3} asks for low on 0.3 and urgent on 0.7, which the cut points 0.5 and 0.5 deliver.

Definition (Natarajan dimension). The Natarajan dimension of H\mathcal HH, written Ndim(H)\mathrm{Ndim}(\mathcal H)Ndim(H), is the largest size of a set C⊆XC \subseteq \mathcal XC⊆X that H\mathcal HH shatters in the multiclass sense, and ∞\infty∞ if there are shattered sets of every finite size. It is named after Natarajan, who introduced it in 1989.

In plain words: the Natarajan dimension is the most messages on which the class can play every two-way choice, with candidates of your choosing. For three urgency folders it is 2. Two things are worth saying about how to check it. First, a lower bound Ndim(H)≥r\mathrm{Ndim}(\mathcal H) \ge rNdim(H)≥r needs just one set of size rrr and one good choice of candidates; an upper bound needs an argument that defeats every set of size r+1r + 1r+1 and every choice of candidates, as the chain argument did. Second, swapping the two candidates of a message only swaps whether it sits in BBB, and BBB ranges over all subsets anyway, so for each message only the unordered pair of candidates matters.

That second remark makes a brute-force checker short. For a finite domain, store each hypothesis as the tuple of its folders, try every set CCC and every choice of one unordered pair of folders per message, and test all mixtures against the restriction:

from itertools import combinations, product

def shatters(H, C, k):
    H_C = {tuple(h[x] for x in C) for h in H}
    pairs = list(combinations(range(1, k + 1), 2))
    return any(all(tuple(p[b] for p, b in zip(fs, B)) in H_C
                   for B in product([0, 1], repeat=len(C)))
               for fs in product(pairs, repeat=len(C)))

def ndim(H, X, k):
    sizes = range(len(X) + 1)
    return max(r for r in sizes if any(
        shatters(H, C, k) for C in combinations(X, r)))

def levels(n, k):
    return [h for h in product(range(1, k + 1), repeat=n)
            if list(h) == sorted(h)]

print([ndim(levels(5, k), range(5), k) for k in (2, 3, 4)])

It prints [1, 2, 3]. Here the domain is five scores in increasing order, levels(5, k) lists every way urgency levels can file them (every non-decreasing tuple of folders), pairs are the unordered candidate pairs, B runs over all mixtures, and ndim returns the largest size of a shattered set. With two, three and four urgency folders the Natarajan dimension is 1, 2 and 3. It looks like k−1k - 1k−1, and it is.

Proposition (urgency levels). For k≥2k \ge 2k≥2 urgency folders on scores in [0,1][0, 1][0,1], Ndim=k−1\mathrm{Ndim} = k - 1Ndim=k−1.

Formally, the class is {ht}\{h_{\mathbf t}\}{ht​} over all cut points t1≤⋯≤tk−1t_1 \le \dots \le t_{k-1}t1​≤⋯≤tk−1​, with

ht(x)=1+∣{j∈[k−1]:x>tj}∣.h_{\mathbf t}(x) = 1 + \left|\{ j \in [k-1] : x > t_j \}\right|.ht​(x)=1+∣{j∈[k−1]:x>tj​}∣.

Inside out: {j∈[k−1]:x>tj}\{ j \in [k-1] : x > t_j \}{j∈[k−1]:x>tj​} is the set of cut points that the score xxx is above (the colon reads “such that”); the bars count them; adding 1 turns “above no cut point” into folder 1. In plain words: a message’s folder is one more than the number of cut points below its score. With cut points 0.5 and 1.0, the score 0.7 is above one cut point, so it goes to folder 2. The levels function of the first snippet is this formula, 1 + sum(x > tj for tj in t).

Proof. Lower bound: take scores 0<c1<⋯<ck−10 < c_1 < \dots < c_{k-1}0<c1​<⋯<ck−1​ and the candidates f0(ci)=if_0(c_i) = if0​(ci​)=i, f1(ci)=i+1f_1(c_i) = i + 1f1​(ci​)=i+1. Any mixture gives cic_ici​ a folder in {i,i+1}\{i, i+1\}{i,i+1}, so the folders never go down as the score goes up: message iii gets at most i+1i + 1i+1 and message i+1i + 1i+1 gets at least i+1i + 1i+1. And every non-decreasing filing ℓ1≤⋯≤ℓr\ell_1 \le \dots \le \ell_rℓ1​≤⋯≤ℓr​ of scores c1<⋯<crc_1 < \dots < c_rc1​<⋯<cr​ is some urgency level: put the cut point tjt_jtj​ at the largest score whose folder is at most jjj, or at 0, below all the scores, if there is none. A score with folder ℓi\ell_iℓi​ is then above exactly the cut points t1,…,tℓi−1t_1, \dots, t_{\ell_i - 1}t1​,…,tℓi​−1​ (for j<ℓij < \ell_ij<ℓi​, the score at tjt_jtj​ has a smaller folder, so it is lower; for j≥ℓij \ge \ell_ij≥ℓi​, tjt_jtj​ is at or above cic_ici​), and the formula gives 1+(ℓi−1)=ℓi1 + (\ell_i - 1) = \ell_i1+(ℓi​−1)=ℓi​. So a set of k−1k - 1k−1 messages is shattered.

Upper bound: suppose rrr scores c1<⋯<crc_1 < \dots < c_rc1​<⋯<cr​ are shattered, with candidates loi<hii\mathrm{lo}_i < \mathrm{hi}_iloi​<hii​. For each i<ri < ri<r, the mixture taking hii\mathrm{hi}_ihii​ on cic_ici​ and loi+1\mathrm{lo}_{i+1}loi+1​ on ci+1c_{i+1}ci+1​ is achieved by some urgency level, which never files a higher score lower, so hii≤loi+1\mathrm{hi}_i \le \mathrm{lo}_{i+1}hii​≤loi+1​. Chaining, 1≤lo1<hi1≤lo2<⋯<hir1 \le \mathrm{lo}_1 < \mathrm{hi}_1 \le \mathrm{lo}_2 < \dots < \mathrm{hi}_r1≤lo1​<hi1​≤lo2​<⋯<hir​, which is rrr strict steps, so hir≥r+1\mathrm{hi}_r \ge r + 1hir​≥r+1. Since hir≤k\mathrm{hi}_r \le khir​≤k, we get r≤k−1r \le k - 1r≤k−1. ■\blacksquare■

With k=2k = 2k=2 folders, urgency levels are lesson 6a’s thresholds, whose VC dimension is 1. That is no coincidence.

Proposition (two labels). If k=2k = 2k=2, then Ndim(H)=VCdim(H)\mathrm{Ndim}(\mathcal H) = \mathrm{VCdim}(\mathcal H)Ndim(H)=VCdim(H).

Proof. With only two labels, f0(x)≠f1(x)f_0(x) \ne f_1(x)f0​(x)=f1​(x) means that {f0(x),f1(x)}\{f_0(x), f_1(x)\}{f0​(x),f1​(x)} is the whole label set at every point. So the mixtures are exactly all 2∣C∣2^{|C|}2∣C∣ labellings of CCC, and H\mathcal HH shatters CCC in the multiclass sense precisely when it produces all of them, which is lesson 6a’s shattering. Conversely, if H\mathcal HH shatters CCC in lesson 6a’s sense, take f0f_0f0​ constantly the first label and f1f_1f1​ constantly the second. The two notions of shattering coincide, so their largest shattered sets do too. ■\blacksquare■

Python can check this on 300 random classes of two-label functions on four points, every subset CCC, comparing the new test with lesson 6a’s count ∣HC∣=2∣C∣|\mathcal H_C| = 2^{|C|}∣HC​∣=2∣C∣:

import random
from itertools import combinations, product

def shatters(H, C, k):
    H_C = {tuple(h[x] for x in C) for h in H}
    pairs = list(combinations(range(1, k + 1), 2))
    return any(all(tuple(p[b] for p, b in zip(fs, B)) in H_C
                   for B in product([0, 1], repeat=len(C)))
               for fs in product(pairs, repeat=len(C)))

def vc_shatters(H, C):
    return len({tuple(h[x] for x in C) for h in H}) == 2 ** len(C)

rng, every = random.Random(1), list(product([1, 2], repeat=4))
sets = [C for r in range(5) for C in combinations(range(4), r)]
classes = [rng.sample(every, rng.randint(1, 16))
           for _ in range(300)]
print(all(shatters(H, C, 2) == vc_shatters(H, C)
          for H in classes for C in sets))

It prints True. So the Natarajan dimension is a genuine generalization: on two labels it is the VC dimension.

Before the formulas take over, play with it. In the lab below, drop messages on the urgency line, choose two candidate folders for each, and watch the grid of mixtures light up as the class achieves them. Then switch to two folders and see lesson 6a come back.

Counting what a class can do: Natarajan’s lemma

Lesson 6b’s proofs ran on one engine: a class of small VC dimension produces few labellings, polynomially many in the number of points instead of exponentially many. Does a small Natarajan dimension buy the same thing?

Before the general statement, a number. The class of all filings of four messages into three folders has 34=813^4 = 8134=81 members and Natarajan dimension 4. A class of Natarajan dimension 1 on four messages and three folders should be much smaller. The lemma below says it has at most 41⋅32=364^1 \cdot 3^2 = 3641⋅32=36 members.

Natarajan’s lemma. Let X\mathcal XX be finite and H⊆[k]X\mathcal H \subseteq [k]^{\mathcal X}H⊆[k]X. Then

∣H∣≤∣X∣Ndim(H)⋅k2 Ndim(H).|\mathcal H| \le |\mathcal X|^{\mathrm{Ndim}(\mathcal H)} \cdot k^{2\,\mathrm{Ndim}(\mathcal H)}.∣H∣≤∣X∣Ndim(H)⋅k2Ndim(H).

Read it from the outside in. ∣H∣|\mathcal H|∣H∣ is the number of hypotheses; ∣X∣|\mathcal X|∣X∣ is the number of messages; Ndim(H)\mathrm{Ndim}(\mathcal H)Ndim(H), say ddd, sits in both exponents; and k2dk^{2d}k2d is (k2)d(k^2)^d(k2)d, one factor k2k^2k2 per dimension, the number of candidate pairs. In plain words: a class of Natarajan dimension ddd on nnn messages has at most ndk2dn^d k^{2d}ndk2d members, a polynomial in nnn instead of knk^nkn. For three urgency folders on five scores, d=2d = 2d=2, the lemma allows 52⋅34=2,0255^2 \cdot 3^4 = 2{,}02552⋅34=2,025; the true count is (72)=21\binom{7}{2} = 21(27​)=21 non-decreasing tuples. Loose, but polynomial, and that is all the proofs need.

The proof is an induction that removes one message at a time, so first the counting step it rests on. Fix one message x0x_0x0​, and let X′=X∖{x0}\mathcal X' = \mathcal X \setminus \{x_0\}X′=X∖{x0​} be the other messages. Every hypothesis, cut down to X′\mathcal X'X′, gives a trace: a function ggg on the other messages. Write HX′\mathcal H_{\mathcal X'}HX′​ for the set of traces. Several hypotheses may leave the same trace, differing only at x0x_0x0​. For two folders i<ji < ji<j, let Hij\mathcal H_{ij}Hij​ be the traces that can be completed both with x0↦ix_0 \mapsto ix0​↦i and with x0↦jx_0 \mapsto jx0​↦j inside H\mathcal HH (here x0↦ix_0 \mapsto ix0​↦i reads “x0x_0x0​ is filed in folder iii”).

Splitting step.

∣H∣≤∣HX′∣+∑1≤i<j≤k∣Hij∣.|\mathcal H| \le |\mathcal H_{\mathcal X'}| + \sum_{1 \le i < j \le k} |\mathcal H_{ij}|.∣H∣≤∣HX′​∣+1≤i<j≤k∑​∣Hij​∣.

The sum runs over every pair of folders i<ji < ji<j, adding up the sizes of the sets Hij\mathcal H_{ij}Hij​. In plain words: the class is at most its traces, plus one extra for every trace and every pair of folders it can put at x0x_0x0​. Take a trace that the class completes in ttt ways, with ttt different folders at x0x_0x0​. It contributes ttt to the left side. On the right it contributes 1 to the first term, plus 1 for each of the t(t−1)/2t(t-1)/2t(t−1)/2 pairs among its ttt folders. And t≤1+t(t−1)/2t \le 1 + t(t-1)/2t≤1+t(t−1)/2 for every whole number t≥1t \ge 1t≥1, because the difference is (t−1)(t−2)/2(t-1)(t-2)/2(t−1)(t−2)/2, which is 0 for t=1t = 1t=1 and t=2t = 2t=2 and positive beyond. A trace with three completions contributes 3 on the left and 1+3=41 + 3 = 41+3=4 on the right. Summing over all traces gives the inequality. Here it is on 1,000 random classes of filings of four messages into three folders, with x0x_0x0​ the first message:

import random
from itertools import combinations, product

rng, n, k = random.Random(2), 4, 3
every = list(product(range(1, k + 1), repeat=n))
holds = []
for _ in range(1000):
    H = set(rng.sample(every, rng.randint(1, 40)))
    rest = {h[1:] for h in H}
    tails = {i: {h[1:] for h in H if h[0] == i}
             for i in range(1, k + 1)}
    both = sum(len(tails[i] & tails[j])
               for i, j in combinations(range(1, k + 1), 2))
    holds.append(len(H) <= len(rest) + both)
print(all(holds), len(holds))

It prints True 1000: every one of the 1,000 classes satisfies the splitting step. rest is HX′\mathcal H_{\mathcal X'}HX′​, tails[i] is the set of traces completed with folder iii, and the intersection tails[i] & tails[j] is Hij\mathcal H_{ij}Hij​.

[diagram:natarajan-split: built on the lesson page]

Proof of Natarajan’s lemma. We prove a slightly more flexible statement: for every whole number d≥0d \ge 0d≥0, every class on n≥1n \ge 1n≥1 messages with Ndim≤d\mathrm{Ndim} \le dNdim≤d has at most ndk2dn^d k^{2d}ndk2d members. The lemma is the case d=Ndim(H)d = \mathrm{Ndim}(\mathcal H)d=Ndim(H). (If X\mathcal XX is empty, there is only one function on it, and the lemma reads 1≤11 \le 11≤1 with the convention 00=10^0 = 100=1.)

Case d=0d = 0d=0. If two hypotheses differed at some message xxx, the single message {x}\{x\}{x} would be shattered with f0(x)f_0(x)f0​(x) and f1(x)f_1(x)f1​(x) the two folders they give it. So all hypotheses agree everywhere, ∣H∣≤1=n0k0|\mathcal H| \le 1 = n^0 k^0∣H∣≤1=n0k0.

Case n=1n = 1n=1, d≥1d \ge 1d≥1. A class on one message has at most kkk members, and k≤k2dk \le k^{2d}k≤k2d.

Induction step, n≥2n \ge 2n≥2, d≥1d \ge 1d≥1. Assume the statement for all classes on n−1n - 1n−1 messages, and apply the splitting step. Two facts about the pieces:

  1. Ndim(HX′)≤d\mathrm{Ndim}(\mathcal H_{\mathcal X'}) \le dNdim(HX′​)≤d. A set C⊆X′C \subseteq \mathcal X'C⊆X′ shattered by the traces, with candidates f0,f1f_0, f_1f0​,f1​, is shattered by H\mathcal HH with the same candidates, because each trace comes from a hypothesis that agrees with it on CCC.
  2. Ndim(Hij)≤d−1\mathrm{Ndim}(\mathcal H_{ij}) \le d - 1Ndim(Hij​)≤d−1. Suppose Hij\mathcal H_{ij}Hij​ shatters C⊆X′C \subseteq \mathcal X'C⊆X′ with candidates f0,f1f_0, f_1f0​,f1​. Extend the candidates to C∪{x0}C \cup \{x_0\}C∪{x0​} by f0(x0)=if_0(x_0) = if0​(x0​)=i and f1(x0)=jf_1(x_0) = jf1​(x0​)=j, which differ. Take any B⊆C∪{x0}B \subseteq C \cup \{x_0\}B⊆C∪{x0​}. Some trace g∈Hijg \in \mathcal H_{ij}g∈Hij​ gives the required mixture on CCC (for the set B∖{x0}B \setminus \{x_0\}B∖{x0​}). Since ggg is in Hij\mathcal H_{ij}Hij​, both completions ggg with x0↦ix_0 \mapsto ix0​↦i and ggg with x0↦jx_0 \mapsto jx0​↦j are in H\mathcal HH: use the first if x0∈Bx_0 \in Bx0​∈B and the second otherwise. So H\mathcal HH shatters C∪{x0}C \cup \{x_0\}C∪{x0​}, a set one larger than CCC. Since H\mathcal HH shatters nothing larger than ddd, ∣C∣+1≤d|C| + 1 \le d∣C∣+1≤d.

By the induction hypothesis on n−1n - 1n−1 messages, ∣HX′∣≤(n−1)dk2d|\mathcal H_{\mathcal X'}| \le (n-1)^d k^{2d}∣HX′​∣≤(n−1)dk2d and each ∣Hij∣≤(n−1)d−1k2(d−1)|\mathcal H_{ij}| \le (n-1)^{d-1} k^{2(d-1)}∣Hij​∣≤(n−1)d−1k2(d−1). There are k(k−1)/2≤k2k(k-1)/2 \le k^2k(k−1)/2≤k2 pairs i<ji < ji<j. So

∣H∣≤(n−1)dk2d+k2(n−1)d−1k2d−2=k2d(n−1)d−1((n−1)+1)=k2d n (n−1)d−1≤k2dnd.|\mathcal H| \le (n-1)^d k^{2d} + k^2 (n-1)^{d-1} k^{2d-2} = k^{2d} (n-1)^{d-1} \big( (n - 1) + 1 \big) = k^{2d}\, n\, (n-1)^{d-1} \le k^{2d} n^d.∣H∣≤(n−1)dk2d+k2(n−1)d−1k2d−2=k2d(n−1)d−1((n−1)+1)=k2dn(n−1)d−1≤k2dnd.

Read the chain left to right: the first term is the bound for the traces; the second is k2k^2k2 pairs times the bound for each Hij\mathcal H_{ij}Hij​; factoring out k2d(n−1)d−1k^{2d}(n-1)^{d-1}k2d(n−1)d−1 leaves (n−1)+1=n(n - 1) + 1 = n(n−1)+1=n; and (n−1)d−1≤nd−1(n-1)^{d-1} \le n^{d-1}(n−1)d−1≤nd−1 finishes it. In plain words: the traces and the pairs together never outgrow ndk2dn^d k^{2d}ndk2d. With n=4n = 4n=4, d=1d = 1d=1, k=3k = 3k=3: k2d n (n−1)d−1=9⋅4⋅1=36=ndk2dk^{2d}\, n\, (n-1)^{d-1} = 9 \cdot 4 \cdot 1 = 36 = n^d k^{2d}k2dn(n−1)d−1=9⋅4⋅1=36=ndk2d, so the last step is an equality there. ■\blacksquare■

Now check the lemma itself on 200 random classes of filings of four messages into three folders, computing each class’s Natarajan dimension by brute force and the worst ratio ∣H∣/(ndk2d)|\mathcal H| / (n^d k^{2d})∣H∣/(ndk2d) for each ddd:

import random
from itertools import combinations as comb, product

def ndim(H, n, k):
    pairs = list(comb(range(1, k + 1), 2))
    def sh(C):
        H_C = {tuple(h[x] for x in C) for h in H}
        return any(all(tuple(p[b] for p, b in zip(fs, B)) in H_C
                       for B in product((0, 1), repeat=len(C)))
                   for fs in product(pairs, repeat=len(C)))
    return max(r for r in range(n + 1)
               if any(sh(C) for C in comb(range(n), r)))

rng, n, k = random.Random(2), 4, 3
every = list(product(range(1, k + 1), repeat=n))
worst = {}
for _ in range(200):
    H = rng.sample(every, rng.randint(1, 30))
    d = ndim(H, n, k)
    r = len(H) / (n ** d * k ** (2 * d))
    worst[d] = round(max(worst.get(d, 0), r), 4)
print(sorted(worst.items()))

It prints [(0, 1.0), (1, 0.1667), (2, 0.017), (3, 0.0006)]. Every ratio is at most 1, as the lemma promises. The ratio 1 at d=0d = 0d=0 is a one-hypothesis class, where the lemma is exact; for larger ddd the bound is generous.

The multiclass fundamental theorem

With a dimension and a counting lemma in hand, the whole of lesson 6a’s theorem comes back, with one new ingredient: the number of folders, kkk, appears, but only inside a logarithm.

The multiclass fundamental theorem. There are absolute constants C1,C2>0C_1, C_2 > 0C1​,C2​>0 such that, for every class H⊆[k]X\mathcal H \subseteq [k]^{\mathcal X}H⊆[k]X with Ndim(H)=d\mathrm{Ndim}(\mathcal H) = dNdim(H)=d:

  1. H\mathcal HH has the uniform convergence property with
C1d+log⁡(1/δ)ε2≤mHUC(ε,δ)≤C2dlog⁡k+log⁡(1/δ)ε2.C_1 \frac{d + \log(1/\delta)}{\varepsilon^2} \le m^{\mathrm{UC}}_{\mathcal H}(\varepsilon, \delta) \le C_2 \frac{d \log k + \log(1/\delta)}{\varepsilon^2}.C1​ε2d+log(1/δ)​≤mHUC​(ε,δ)≤C2​ε2dlogk+log(1/δ)​.
  1. H\mathcal HH is agnostic PAC learnable with
C1d+log⁡(1/δ)ε2≤mH(ε,δ)≤C2dlog⁡k+log⁡(1/δ)ε2.C_1 \frac{d + \log(1/\delta)}{\varepsilon^2} \le m_{\mathcal H}(\varepsilon, \delta) \le C_2 \frac{d \log k + \log(1/\delta)}{\varepsilon^2}.C1​ε2d+log(1/δ)​≤mH​(ε,δ)≤C2​ε2dlogk+log(1/δ)​.
  1. H\mathcal HH is PAC learnable (assuming realizability) with
C1d+log⁡(1/δ)ε≤mH(ε,δ)≤C2dlog⁡(kd/ε)+log⁡(1/δ)ε.C_1 \frac{d + \log(1/\delta)}{\varepsilon} \le m_{\mathcal H}(\varepsilon, \delta) \le C_2 \frac{d \log\left( kd/\varepsilon \right) + \log(1/\delta)}{\varepsilon}.C1​εd+log(1/δ)​≤mH​(ε,δ)≤C2​εdlog(kd/ε)+log(1/δ)​.

All three have the same anatomy, so read the second from the inside out.

  • ddd is the Natarajan dimension, playing exactly the role the VC dimension played in lesson 6a.
  • log⁡(1/δ)\log(1/\delta)log(1/δ) is the price of confidence; log⁡\loglog is the natural logarithm throughout.
  • dlog⁡kd \log kdlogk is new: the dimension, multiplied by the logarithm of the number of folders. Going from 300 folders to 3,000 multiplies log⁡k\log klogk by about 1.4, not by 10.
  • Dividing by ε2\varepsilon^2ε2 means halving the tolerance quadruples the labels; in the third line, where some hypothesis is perfect, the division is by ε\varepsilonε, and the extra log⁡(kd/ε)\log(kd/\varepsilon)log(kd/ε) is the logarithm of the folder count times the dimension over the tolerance.
  • C1C_1C1​ and C2C_2C2​ are absolute constants: fixed numbers, the same for every class, every kkk, every distribution. The theorem says they exist but not what they are; as in lesson 28, the floors hold for small enough ε\varepsilonε and δ\deltaδ.
  • mHUCm^{\mathrm{UC}}_{\mathcal H}mHUC​ is lesson 4’s uniform-convergence sample size, the examples needed for every hypothesis’s empirical risk to be within ε\varepsilonε of its true risk with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ; mHm_{\mathcal H}mH​ is the learning one.

In plain words: a multiclass class is learnable exactly when its Natarajan dimension is finite, and the labels it needs grow with that dimension, plus the log of one over the failure chance, divided by the tolerance squared, with a logarithmic factor such as log⁡k\log klogk between the floor and the ceiling. For your 300-folder filter, the next section will show that ddd is at most 300×30=9,000300 \times 30 = 9{,}000300×30=9,000. Without the unknown constants, at ε=δ=0.05\varepsilon = \delta = 0.05ε=δ=0.05:

from math import log

k, n, eps, delta = 300, 30, 0.05, 0.05
d = k * n
lower = (d + log(1 / delta)) / eps ** 2
upper = (d * log(k) + log(1 / delta)) / eps ** 2
pac_low = (d + log(1 / delta)) / eps
pac_up = (d * log(k * d / eps) + log(1 / delta)) / eps
print(d, round(lower), round(upper), round(upper / lower, 2))
print(round(pac_low), round(pac_up), round(pac_up / pac_low, 2))

It prints 9000 3601198 20534815 5.7, then 180060 3204869 17.8. In the agnostic case, the floor is a constant times 3.6 million and the ceiling a constant times 20.5 million, a gap of the factor log⁡300≈5.7\log 300 \approx 5.7log300≈5.7. In the realizable case the floor is a constant times 180,060 and the ceiling a constant times 3.2 million. These are the shapes the review needed. For a concrete budget we’ll need numbers without unknown constants; the last sections of this lesson produce some.

### Why the upper bounds hold

Before lesson 28, lesson 6b proved a weaker form of the theorem (with 1/δ1/\delta1/δ where log⁡(1/δ)\log(1/\delta)log(1/δ) belongs, the price of Markov’s inequality) through a theorem we can reuse almost untouched: uniform convergence from a small growth function. It said that with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ, every hhh has ∣LD(h)−LS(h)∣≤(4+2log⁡τH(2m))/(δ2m)|L_{\mathcal D}(h) - L_S(h)| \le (4 + 2\sqrt{\log \tau_{\mathcal H}(2m)})/(\delta\sqrt{2m})∣LD​(h)−LS​(h)∣≤(4+2logτH​(2m)​)/(δ2m​), where the growth function τH(2m)\tau_{\mathcal H}(2m)τH​(2m) is the largest restriction ∣HC∣|\mathcal H_C|∣HC​∣ over sets CCC of 2m2m2m points. Look back at Step 4 of its proof. The only thing it used about the class was that, once the 2m2m2m training and ghost examples are fixed, each example’s 0-1 loss depends on hhh only through hhh’s label on that example’s message, so the number of distinct loss vectors is at most ∣HC∣|\mathcal H_C|∣HC​∣. That is just as true with 300 folders: whether hhh files message xix_ixi​ correctly depends only on h(xi)h(x_i)h(xi​). So the same theorem holds for multiclass classes, with τH(2m)\tau_{\mathcal H}(2m)τH​(2m) counting folder vectors.

Now apply Natarajan’s lemma to the restriction HC\mathcal H_CHC​, a class on the at most 2m2m2m messages of CCC. It cannot shatter more than H\mathcal HH does, so its Natarajan dimension is at most ddd, and ∣HC∣≤(2m)dk2d|\mathcal H_C| \le (2m)^d k^{2d}∣HC​∣≤(2m)dk2d. Taking logs, log⁡τH(2m)≤dlog⁡(2m)+2dlog⁡k\log \tau_{\mathcal H}(2m) \le d \log(2m) + 2d \log klogτH​(2m)≤dlog(2m)+2dlogk, and with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ, for every h∈Hh \in \mathcal Hh∈H,

∣LD(h)−LS(h)∣≤4+2dlog⁡(2m)+2dlog⁡kδ2m.|L_{\mathcal D}(h) - L_S(h)| \le \frac{4 + 2\sqrt{d \log(2m) + 2d \log k}}{\delta\sqrt{2m}}.∣LD​(h)−LS​(h)∣≤δ2m​4+2dlog(2m)+2dlogk​​.

From the inside out: dlog⁡(2m)+2dlog⁡kd\log(2m) + 2d\log kdlog(2m)+2dlogk is the log of Natarajan’s count on 2m2m2m messages; its square root, doubled and plus 4, is the numerator from lesson 6b; δ2m\delta\sqrt{2m}δ2m​ underneath shrinks the bound as labels grow. In plain words: every hypothesis’s training score is within a quantity that shrinks like d(log⁡m+log⁡k)/m\sqrt{d(\log m + \log k)/m}d(logm+logk)/m​ of its true score, with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ. For three urgency folders (d=2d = 2d=2, k=3k = 3k=3) at δ=0.1\delta = 0.1δ=0.1:

from math import log, sqrt

def uc_bound(m, d, k, delta):
    log_tau = d * log(2 * m) + 2 * d * log(k)
    return (4 + 2 * sqrt(log_tau)) / (delta * sqrt(2 * m))

d, k, delta = 2, 3, 0.1
for m in (10 ** 3, 10 ** 5, 10 ** 7):
    print(m, round(uc_bound(m, d, k, delta), 4))

It prints 1000 2.8741, 100000 0.3295 and 10000000 0.0365. Useless at a thousand labels, but it goes to zero as mmm grows, which is all a uniform convergence property needs: for any ε\varepsilonε there is an mmm beyond which the bound is under ε\varepsilonε. So finite Natarajan dimension and finitely many folders give uniform convergence, and by lesson 4 any ERM is then a successful agnostic learner. The sharper rates come from running lesson 28’s proofs with Natarajan’s (2m)dk2d(2m)^d k^{2d}(2m)dk2d in the place of Sauer’s (2em/d)d(2em/d)^d(2em/d)d: its ε\varepsilonε-net argument gives the realizable ceiling, dlog⁡(kd/ε)d\log(kd/\varepsilon)dlog(kd/ε) and all, and its Rademacher argument gives an agnostic ceiling with dlog⁡(kd/ε)d\log(kd/\varepsilon)dlog(kd/ε) where the theorem has dlog⁡kd\log kdlogk (Problem 3). Removing that extra log⁡(d/ε)\log(d/\varepsilon)log(d/ε) needs the chaining that lesson 28 left unproved for two labels too.

### Why the lower bounds hold

The floors come from the two-label theorem by a disguise. Suppose Ndim(H)=d\mathrm{Ndim}(\mathcal H) = dNdim(H)=d, witnessed by a set CCC of ddd messages and candidates f0,f1f_0, f_1f0​,f1​. Picture a two-label problem on CCC: each message’s label is 1 (“it belongs in its first candidate”) or 0 (“in its second”). Any multiclass learner for H\mathcal HH can be turned into a two-label learner for the class of all yes/no functions on CCC, whose VC dimension is ddd, and a learner for that class cannot beat lesson 28’s two-label floor, (d+log⁡(1/δ))/(1024 ε2)(d + \log(1/\delta))/(1024\,\varepsilon^2)(d+log(1/δ))/(1024ε2) for ε≤1/(82)\varepsilon \le 1/(8\sqrt2)ε≤1/(82​) and δ≤1/8\delta \le 1/8δ≤1/8.

Proposition (the disguise). Fix C,f0,f1C, f_0, f_1C,f0​,f1​ as above and let AAA be any multiclass learner. Define a two-label learner A′A'A′: given yes/no examples (x,b)(x, b)(x,b) with x∈Cx \in Cx∈C, relabel each as (x,f0(x))(x, f_0(x))(x,f0​(x)) if b=1b = 1b=1 and (x,f1(x))(x, f_1(x))(x,f1​(x)) if b=0b = 0b=0, run AAA to get hhh, and return g(x)=1[h(x)=f0(x)]g(x) = \mathbb 1[h(x) = f_0(x)]g(x)=1[h(x)=f0​(x)]. Then for every distribution D′\mathcal D'D′ on C×{0,1}C \times \{0, 1\}C×{0,1}, with D\mathcal DD the relabelled distribution, LD′(g)−min⁡b′LD′(b′)≤LD(h)−min⁡h′∈HLD(h′)L_{\mathcal D'}(g) - \min_{b'} L_{\mathcal D'}(b') \le L_{\mathcal D}(h) - \min_{h' \in \mathcal H} L_{\mathcal D}(h')LD′​(g)−minb′​LD′​(b′)≤LD​(h)−minh′∈H​LD​(h′), where b′b'b′ ranges over all yes/no functions on CCC.

Here 1[⋅]\mathbb 1[\cdot]1[⋅] is the indicator, 1 when the statement inside holds and 0 otherwise, so ggg says yes exactly when hhh picked the first candidate; min⁡\minmin is the smallest true risk in a class. In plain words: the disguised learner’s excess risk is never more than the multiclass learner’s.

Proof. Two pointwise facts. First, ggg errs only where hhh errs. On an example whose label is the first candidate, ggg is wrong exactly when h(x)≠f0(x)h(x) \ne f_0(x)h(x)=f0​(x), that is, exactly when hhh is wrong. On an example whose label is the second candidate, ggg is wrong when h(x)=f0(x)h(x) = f_0(x)h(x)=f0​(x), and then h(x)≠f1(x)h(x) \ne f_1(x)h(x)=f1​(x), so hhh is wrong too. Taking expectations, LD′(g)≤LD(h)L_{\mathcal D'}(g) \le L_{\mathcal D}(h)LD′​(g)≤LD​(h).

Second, the best yes/no function is no better than the best multiclass hypothesis. For each yes/no function b′b'b′ on CCC, shattering gives an h′∈Hh' \in \mathcal Hh′∈H taking f0f_0f0​ where b′=1b' = 1b′=1 and f1f_1f1​ where b′=0b' = 0b′=0. Since h′(x)h'(x)h′(x) is always one of the two candidates, h′h'h′ is wrong on an example exactly when b′b'b′ is, so LD(h′)=LD′(b′)L_{\mathcal D}(h') = L_{\mathcal D'}(b')LD​(h′)=LD′​(b′), and therefore min⁡h′LD(h′)≤min⁡b′LD′(b′)\min_{h'} L_{\mathcal D}(h') \le \min_{b'} L_{\mathcal D'}(b')minh′​LD​(h′)≤minb′​LD′​(b′). Subtracting the second fact from the first gives the claim. ■\blacksquare■

Here are both pointwise facts on 100,000 random examples with five folders:

import random

rng, k, n = random.Random(0), 5, 100_000
g_errs = h_errs = g_only = 0
for _ in range(n):
    f0, f1 = rng.sample(range(1, k + 1), 2)
    y, h = rng.choice([f0, f1]), rng.randint(1, k)
    g_wrong = (h == f0) != (y == f0)
    g_errs, h_errs = g_errs + g_wrong, h_errs + (h != y)
    g_only += g_wrong and h == y
print(round(g_errs / n, 4), round(h_errs / n, 4), g_only)

It prints 0.5014 0.8014 0: the disguised learner errs on about half the examples and the multiclass one on about 80%, and the last number counts examples where ggg erred but hhh did not. There are none.

So if AAA agnostically learns H\mathcal HH with mmm examples, then A′A'A′ agnostically learns a two-label class of VC dimension ddd with mmm examples, and lesson 28’s floor forces m≥(d+log⁡(1/δ))/(1024 ε2)m \ge (d + \log(1/\delta))/(1024\,\varepsilon^2)m≥(d+log(1/δ))/(1024ε2), so C1=1/1024C_1 = 1/1024C1​=1/1024 works here too. In the realizable case the same disguise works: if D′\mathcal D'D′ is labelled by some b′b'b′, then D\mathcal DD is labelled by the matching h′h'h′, and LD′(g)≤LD(h)L_{\mathcal D'}(g) \le L_{\mathcal D}(h)LD′​(g)≤LD​(h), so any two-label realizable floor carries over; the one lesson 6a stated has ε\varepsilonε in place of ε2\varepsilon^2ε2 (lesson 28 left only its log⁡(1/δ)\log(1/\delta)log(1/δ) part, as a problem). For uniform convergence, recall from lesson 4 that an ε/2\varepsilon/2ε/2-representative sample makes any ERM ε\varepsilonε-accurate, so mH(ε,δ)≤mHUC(ε/2,δ)m_{\mathcal H}(\varepsilon, \delta) \le m^{\mathrm{UC}}_{\mathcal H}(\varepsilon/2, \delta)mH​(ε,δ)≤mHUC​(ε/2,δ). Writing ε′\varepsilon'ε′ for ε/2\varepsilon/2ε/2, mHUC(ε′,δ)≥mH(2ε′,δ)≥C1(d+log⁡(1/δ))/(4ε′2)m^{\mathrm{UC}}_{\mathcal H}(\varepsilon', \delta) \ge m_{\mathcal H}(2\varepsilon', \delta) \ge C_1 (d + \log(1/\delta))/(4\varepsilon'^2)mHUC​(ε′,δ)≥mH​(2ε′,δ)≥C1​(d+log(1/δ))/(4ε′2): the first floor, with the constant divided by 4.

Calculating the Natarajan dimension

A dimension is only useful if you can compute it, or at least bound it, for the classes you actually use. Here is the pattern you will see three times: the Natarajan dimension tends to be about the number of parameters it takes to write a hypothesis down.

### One-versus-all

Recall lesson 17a’s one-versus-all: train one yes/no filter per folder, “is it folder iii or not?”, and file a message in a folder whose filter says yes, breaking ties (several yeses, or none) by the smallest folder number. Lesson 17a wrote the answers as +1+1+1 and −1-1−1; here yes is 1 and no is 0, which picks the same folder. If each yes/no filter comes from a class Hbin\mathcal H_{\mathrm{bin}}Hbin​ of VC dimension ddd, the multiclass class is

HbinOvA,k={T(h1,…,hk):h1,…,hk∈Hbin},T(h1,…,hk)(x)=argmax⁡i∈[k]hi(x).\mathcal H^{\mathrm{OvA}, k}_{\mathrm{bin}} = \left\{ T(h_1, \dots, h_k) : h_1, \dots, h_k \in \mathcal H_{\mathrm{bin}} \right\}, \qquad T(h_1, \dots, h_k)(x) = \operatorname*{argmax}_{i \in [k]} h_i(x).HbinOvA,k​={T(h1​,…,hk​):h1​,…,hk​∈Hbin​},T(h1​,…,hk​)(x)=i∈[k]argmax​hi​(x).

Inside out: hi(x)h_i(x)hi​(x) is filter iii’s answer, 1 or 0; argmax⁡i∈[k]\operatorname{argmax}_{i \in [k]}argmaxi∈[k]​ is the folder number whose answer is largest, with ties to the smallest number; T(h1,…,hk)T(h_1, \dots, h_k)T(h1​,…,hk​) is the folder rule built from the kkk filters; and the braces collect it over every choice of kkk filters from Hbin\mathcal H_{\mathrm{bin}}Hbin​. In plain words: the class of every filer you can assemble from kkk yes/no filters, one per folder. With filters answering 0, 1, 1, 0 for a message, the largest answer is 1, shared by folders 2 and 3, and the message goes to folder 2.

How big should its Natarajan dimension be? A hypothesis takes kkk filters to write down, each with “ddd parameters’ worth” of freedom, so about kdkdkd. That is the right size, up to a logarithm. To prove it, we will use Sauer’s lemma in a form that holds for every ccc, not only c≥dc \ge dc≥d: a class of VC dimension ddd produces at most ∑i≤d(ci)≤(c+1)d\sum_{i \le d}\binom{c}{i} \le (c + 1)^d∑i≤d​(ic​)≤(c+1)d labellings of ccc points. (Each (ci)≤ci≤(di)ci\binom{c}{i} \le c^i \le \binom{d}{i} c^i(ic​)≤ci≤(id​)ci, and the binomial theorem sums ∑i≤d(di)ci\sum_{i \le d} \binom{d}{i} c^i∑i≤d​(id​)ci to (c+1)d(c + 1)^d(c+1)d.)

### General reductions

One-versus-all is one of many multiclass-to-binary reductions: train lll yes/no filters, and let a fixed rule r:{0,1}l→[k]r: \{0,1\}^l \to [k]r:{0,1}l→[k] turn their lll answers into a folder. All-pairs from lesson 17a is another, with l=(k2)l = \binom{k}{2}l=(2k​). The class is

Hbinr={R(h1,…,hl):h1,…,hl∈Hbin},R(h1,…,hl)(x)=r(h1(x),…,hl(x)).\mathcal H^{r}_{\mathrm{bin}} = \left\{ R(h_1, \dots, h_l) : h_1, \dots, h_l \in \mathcal H_{\mathrm{bin}} \right\}, \qquad R(h_1, \dots, h_l)(x) = r\big(h_1(x), \dots, h_l(x)\big).Hbinr​={R(h1​,…,hl​):h1​,…,hl​∈Hbin​},R(h1​,…,hl​)(x)=r(h1​(x),…,hl​(x)).

Inside out: the lll filters answer, rrr reads the vector of answers and names a folder, and the braces collect every such rule. In plain words: every filer you can build by asking lll yes/no filters and combining their answers with a fixed rule. One-versus-all is the case l=kl = kl=k, with rrr returning the position of the first 1, or 1 if there is none.

Lemma (reductions). If VCdim(Hbin)=d\mathrm{VCdim}(\mathcal H_{\mathrm{bin}}) = dVCdim(Hbin​)=d and ld≥4ld \ge 4ld≥4, then Ndim(Hbinr)≤3 ldlog⁡(ld)\mathrm{Ndim}(\mathcal H^{r}_{\mathrm{bin}}) \le 3\, l d \log(l d)Ndim(Hbinr​)≤3ldlog(ld). In particular, Ndim(HbinOvA,k)≤3kdlog⁡(kd)\mathrm{Ndim}(\mathcal H^{\mathrm{OvA},k}_{\mathrm{bin}}) \le 3kd\log(kd)Ndim(HbinOvA,k​)≤3kdlog(kd) when kd≥4kd \ge 4kd≥4.

In plain words: a reduction that asks lll filters of VC dimension ddd has Natarajan dimension at most about 3ldlog⁡(ld)3ld\log(ld)3ldlog(ld). For 300 one-versus-all filters from a class of VC dimension d=30d = 30d=30, that is 3×9,000×log⁡9,000≈245,8003 \times 9{,}000 \times \log 9{,}000 \approx 245{,}8003×9,000×log9,000≈245,800.

Proof. Let CCC be shattered, and count the folder vectors ∣(Hbinr)C∣|(\mathcal H^r_{\mathrm{bin}})_C|∣(Hbinr​)C​∣ two ways.

From below: the 2∣C∣2^{|C|}2∣C∣ mixtures are all different vectors on CCC, because f0(x)≠f1(x)f_0(x) \ne f_1(x)f0​(x)=f1​(x) at every message, so two different sets BBB give vectors that differ somewhere. Each is achieved, so ∣(Hbinr)C∣≥2∣C∣|(\mathcal H^r_{\mathrm{bin}})_C| \ge 2^{|C|}∣(Hbinr​)C​∣≥2∣C∣.

From above: a rule’s folders on CCC are determined by its lll filters’ answers on CCC, which are lll labellings from (Hbin)C(\mathcal H_{\mathrm{bin}})_C(Hbin​)C​. There are at most ∣(Hbin)C∣l|(\mathcal H_{\mathrm{bin}})_C|^l∣(Hbin​)C​∣l ways to choose them, and Sauer gives ∣(Hbin)C∣≤(∣C∣+1)d|(\mathcal H_{\mathrm{bin}})_C| \le (|C| + 1)^d∣(Hbin​)C​∣≤(∣C∣+1)d. Together,

2∣C∣≤∣(Hbinr)C∣≤∣(Hbin)C∣l≤(∣C∣+1)ld.2^{|C|} \le \left|(\mathcal H^r_{\mathrm{bin}})_C\right| \le \left|(\mathcal H_{\mathrm{bin}})_C\right|^{l} \le (|C| + 1)^{ld}.2∣C∣≤∣(Hbinr​)C​∣≤∣(Hbin​)C​∣l≤(∣C∣+1)ld.

In plain words: a shattered set needs 2∣C∣2^{|C|}2∣C∣ folder vectors, but lll filters can only produce polynomially many. The condition D≥4D \ge 4D≥4 is real, not decoration: for D=1D = 1D=1, 222 and 333, the inequality clog⁡2≤Dlog⁡(c+1)c\log 2 \le D\log(c+1)clog2≤Dlog(c+1) allows sets larger than 3Dlog⁡D3D\log D3DlogD. Here is the largest ccc it allows, next to 3Dlog⁡D3D\log D3DlogD, and the last step checked numerically:

from math import log

def largest_c(D):
    c = 0
    while (c + 1) * log(2) <= D * log(c + 2):
        c += 1
    return c

for D in (1, 2, 3, 4, 10, 300, 9000):
    print(D, largest_c(D), round(3 * D * log(D), 1))
print(all(D ** (3 * log(2)) >= 3 * D * log(D) + 1
          for D in range(4, 10 ** 5)))

It prints

1 1 0.0
2 5 4.2
3 10 9.9
4 16 16.6
10 59 69.1
300 3536 5133.4
9000 155193 245834.5
True

From D=4D = 4D=4 on, the counting argument never allows more than 3Dlog⁡D3D\log D3DlogD; at 1, 2 and 3 it does, which is why the lemma asks for ld≥4ld \ge 4ld≥4.

How tight is it? Take one-versus-all with k=4k = 4k=4 folders over lesson 6a’s thresholds (VC dimension 1) on six scores. Python builds every rule from every choice of four thresholds and computes the Natarajan dimension by brute force:

from itertools import combinations as comb, product

def ndim(H, n, k):
    pairs = list(comb(range(1, k + 1), 2))
    def sh(C):
        H_C = {tuple(h[x] for x in C) for h in H}
        return any(all(tuple(p[b] for p, b in zip(fs, B)) in H_C
                       for B in product((0, 1), repeat=len(C)))
                   for fs in product(pairs, repeat=len(C)))
    return max(r for r in range(n + 1)
               if any(sh(C) for C in comb(range(n), r)))

n, k = 6, 4
H_bin = [tuple(int(x > t) for x in range(n))
         for t in range(-1, n)]

def T(hs):
    return tuple(1 + max(range(k), key=lambda i: (hs[i][x], -i))
                 for x in range(n))

H_ova = {T(hs) for hs in product(H_bin, repeat=k)}
print(len(H_bin), len(H_bin) ** k, len(H_ova), ndim(H_ova, n, k))

It prints 7 2401 204 4. Seven threshold labellings of six scores, 74=2,4017^4 = 2{,}40174=2,401 ways to choose four filters, but only 204 distinct folder rules: different choices often file every message the same way. The Natarajan dimension is 4, equal to kdkdkd, and well under the lemma’s 3⋅4⋅log⁡4≈16.63 \cdot 4 \cdot \log 4 \approx 16.63⋅4⋅log4≈16.6. For some binary classes one-versus-all is far smaller than kdkdkd (Problem 1), and for halfspaces it really is of order kdkdkd (Problem 2).

### Linear multiclass predictors

Your 300-folder filter is not a reduction; it is lesson 17a’s linear multiclass predictor, the class HΨ,W\mathcal H_{\Psi, W}HΨ,W​ with every weight vector allowed, W=RdW = \mathbb R^dW=Rd. In this section, as in lesson 17a, ddd is the length of the feature vectors, not a dimension of a class. Recall: a class-sensitive feature mapping Ψ:X×[k]→Rd\Psi: \mathcal X \times [k] \to \mathbb R^dΨ:X×[k]→Rd turns a message xxx and a candidate folder iii into a vector Ψ(x,i)\Psi(x, i)Ψ(x,i) of ddd numbers; a weight vector w∈Rd\mathbf w \in \mathbb R^dw∈Rd scores the pair by the inner product ⟨w,Ψ(x,i)⟩\langle \mathbf w, \Psi(x, i) \rangle⟨w,Ψ(x,i)⟩ (multiply matching entries and add); and the predictor files the message in the folder with the highest score. The class is

HΨ={x↦argmax⁡i∈[k]⟨w,Ψ(x,i)⟩  :  w∈Rd}.\mathcal H_\Psi = \left\{ x \mapsto \operatorname*{argmax}_{i \in [k]} \langle \mathbf w, \Psi(x, i) \rangle \;:\; \mathbf w \in \mathbb R^d \right\}.HΨ​={x↦i∈[k]argmax​⟨w,Ψ(x,i)⟩:w∈Rd}.

Inside out: for a message xxx, compute all kkk scores ⟨w,Ψ(x,i)⟩\langle \mathbf w, \Psi(x, i)\rangle⟨w,Ψ(x,i)⟩; argmax⁡\operatorname{argmax}argmax picks the folder with the largest score, and as with one-versus-all we break ties by the smallest folder number; x↦…x \mapsto \dotsx↦… (“xxx goes to …”) names the resulting function; the braces collect one such function per weight vector w\mathbf ww, where Rd\mathbb R^dRd is the set of all vectors of ddd real numbers. In plain words: one hypothesis per weight vector, each filing a message in its highest-scoring folder. Each hypothesis is written down with ddd numbers, so you might guess Ndim≤d\mathrm{Ndim} \le dNdim≤d. That guess is exactly right.

Theorem (linear multiclass predictors). Ndim(HΨ)≤d\mathrm{Ndim}(\mathcal H_\Psi) \le dNdim(HΨ​)≤d.

The idea is to turn each shattered message into a vector, the difference between its two candidates’ feature vectors, and to notice that “the first candidate wins” is a halfspace question about that difference. Then a lemma about halfspaces finishes the job.

Lemma (no d+1d + 1d+1 vectors). No d+1d + 1d+1 vectors u1,…,ud+1∈Rd\mathbf u_1, \dots, \mathbf u_{d+1} \in \mathbb R^du1​,…,ud+1​∈Rd are shattered by the class of yes/no rules v↦1[⟨w,v⟩≥0]\mathbf v \mapsto \mathbb 1[\langle \mathbf w, \mathbf v \rangle \ge 0]v↦1[⟨w,v⟩≥0], w∈Rd\mathbf w \in \mathbb R^dw∈Rd.

Proof. Any d+1d + 1d+1 vectors in Rd\mathbb R^dRd are linearly dependent: there are numbers a1,…,ad+1a_1, \dots, a_{d+1}a1​,…,ad+1​, not all zero, with ∑iaiui=0\sum_i a_i \mathbf u_i = \mathbf 0∑i​ai​ui​=0. Flipping the signs of all the aia_iai​ if necessary, the set I={i:ai>0}I = \{i : a_i > 0\}I={i:ai​>0} is not empty; let J={i:ai<0}J = \{i : a_i < 0\}J={i:ai​<0}. Suppose some w\mathbf ww labels every ui\mathbf u_iui​ with i∈Ii \in Ii∈I as 0 (so ⟨w,ui⟩<0\langle \mathbf w, \mathbf u_i \rangle < 0⟨w,ui​⟩<0) and every uj\mathbf u_juj​ with j∈Jj \in Jj∈J as 1 (so ⟨w,uj⟩≥0\langle \mathbf w, \mathbf u_j \rangle \ge 0⟨w,uj​⟩≥0). Then

0=⟨w,∑iaiui⟩=∑i∈Iai⟨w,ui⟩+∑j∈Jaj⟨w,uj⟩<0,0 = \Big\langle \mathbf w, \sum_i a_i \mathbf u_i \Big\rangle = \sum_{i \in I} a_i \langle \mathbf w, \mathbf u_i \rangle + \sum_{j \in J} a_j \langle \mathbf w, \mathbf u_j \rangle < 0,0=⟨w,i∑​ai​ui​⟩=i∈I∑​ai​⟨w,ui​⟩+j∈J∑​aj​⟨w,uj​⟩<0,

because the first sum has at least one term, each positive times negative, and the second has terms negative times non-negative. Here ∑i∈I\sum_{i \in I}∑i∈I​ adds over the indices in III. In plain words: the dependency forbids one particular labelling, so the vectors are not shattered. ■\blacksquare■

For u1=(1,0)\mathbf u_1 = (1, 0)u1​=(1,0), u2=(0,1)\mathbf u_2 = (0, 1)u2​=(0,1), u3=(1,1)\mathbf u_3 = (1, 1)u3​=(1,1), the dependency is u1+u2−u3=0\mathbf u_1 + \mathbf u_2 - \mathbf u_3 = \mathbf 0u1​+u2​−u3​=0, so the forbidden labelling is “0, 0, 1”. A hundred thousand random w\mathbf ww agree:

import random

u = [(1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1)]
rng, seen = random.Random(0), set()
for _ in range(100_000):
    w = (rng.uniform(-1, 1), rng.uniform(-1, 1))
    seen.add(tuple(int(w[0] * a + w[1] * b >= 0) for a, b in u))
print(len(seen), sorted(set(
    (a, b, c) for a in (0, 1) for b in (0, 1) for c in (0, 1))
    - seen))

It prints 6 [(0, 0, 1), (1, 1, 0)]: six of the eight labellings appear, and the two missing are the one the proof forbids and its mirror, which comes from the same dependency with the signs flipped.

Proof of the theorem. Let CCC be shattered by HΨ\mathcal H_\PsiHΨ​ with candidates f0,f1f_0, f_1f0​,f1​. For each x∈Cx \in Cx∈C define the difference vector

ρ(x)=Ψ(x,f0(x))−Ψ(x,f1(x)),\rho(x) = \Psi(x, f_0(x)) - \Psi(x, f_1(x)),ρ(x)=Ψ(x,f0​(x))−Ψ(x,f1​(x)),

the feature vector of the first candidate minus that of the second. Then ⟨w,ρ(x)⟩\langle \mathbf w, \rho(x) \rangle⟨w,ρ(x)⟩ is the first candidate’s score minus the second’s: positive means the first candidate is ahead.

Now the ties. Split CCC into C<C_<C<​, the messages whose first candidate has the smaller folder number, and C>C_>C>​, the rest. Take a hypothesis with weights w\mathbf ww that picks one of the two candidates at xxx.

  • If x∈C<x \in C_<x∈C<​: picking f0(x)f_0(x)f0​(x) means its score is the largest, so ⟨w,ρ(x)⟩≥0\langle \mathbf w, \rho(x) \rangle \ge 0⟨w,ρ(x)⟩≥0. Picking f1(x)f_1(x)f1​(x) means f1(x)f_1(x)f1​(x) has the largest score and no smaller folder number ties it; f0(x)f_0(x)f0​(x) has a smaller number, so its score is strictly lower: ⟨w,ρ(x)⟩<0\langle \mathbf w, \rho(x) \rangle < 0⟨w,ρ(x)⟩<0.
  • If x∈C>x \in C_>x∈C>​: by the same reasoning with the roles swapped, picking f1(x)f_1(x)f1​(x) means ⟨w,−ρ(x)⟩≥0\langle \mathbf w, -\rho(x) \rangle \ge 0⟨w,−ρ(x)⟩≥0, and picking f0(x)f_0(x)f0​(x) means ⟨w,−ρ(x)⟩<0\langle \mathbf w, -\rho(x) \rangle < 0⟨w,−ρ(x)⟩<0.

So set u(x)=ρ(x)\mathbf u(x) = \rho(x)u(x)=ρ(x) on C<C_<C<​ and u(x)=−ρ(x)\mathbf u(x) = -\rho(x)u(x)=−ρ(x) on C>C_>C>​. The yes/no rule 1[⟨w,u(x)⟩≥0]\mathbb 1[\langle \mathbf w, \mathbf u(x) \rangle \ge 0]1[⟨w,u(x)⟩≥0] says yes exactly on the messages of C<C_<C<​ where f0f_0f0​ was picked and the messages of C>C_>C>​ where f1f_1f1​ was picked. As BBB runs over all subsets of CCC, that yes-set, (B∩C<)∪(C>∖B)(B \cap C_<) \cup (C_> \setminus B)(B∩C<​)∪(C>​∖B), also runs over all subsets of CCC (the map flips membership on C>C_>C>​ and keeps it on C<C_<C<​, and doing it twice gives BBB back). So the vectors u(x)\mathbf u(x)u(x) are shattered by the yes/no rules of the lemma. They are also all different: two messages with the same vector would always get the same answer, and could not be split. By the lemma there are at most ddd of them, so ∣C∣≤d|C| \le d∣C∣≤d. ■\blacksquare■

For your filter, Ψ\PsiΨ is the multivector construction of lesson 17a: with messages x∈Rn\mathbf x \in \mathbb R^nx∈Rn and kkk folders, Ψ(x,y)∈Rkn\Psi(\mathbf x, y) \in \mathbb R^{kn}Ψ(x,y)∈Rkn is kkk blocks of nnn entries, all zero except block yyy, which holds x\mathbf xx:

Ψ(x,y)=[ 0,…,0⏟(y−1)n, x1,…,xn⏟n, 0,…,0⏟(k−y)n ].\Psi(\mathbf x, y) = \big[\, \underbrace{0, \dots, 0}_{(y-1)n},\ \underbrace{x_1, \dots, x_n}_{n},\ \underbrace{0, \dots, 0}_{(k-y)n} \,\big].Ψ(x,y)=[(y−1)n0,…,0​​, nx1​,…,xn​​​, (k−y)n0,…,0​​].

The braces underneath count the entries: (y−1)n(y-1)n(y−1)n zeros for the blocks before yyy, the nnn features, then (k−y)n(k-y)n(k−y)n zeros. Writing w\mathbf ww as kkk blocks w1,…,wk\mathbf w_1, \dots, \mathbf w_kw1​,…,wk​, the score of folder yyy is ⟨wy,x⟩\langle \mathbf w_y, \mathbf x \rangle⟨wy​,x⟩. In plain words: one weight vector per folder, and each folder scores the message with its own. With k=300k = 300k=300 and n=30n = 30n=30, Ψ\PsiΨ has 9,0009{,}0009,000 entries.

Corollary (multivector). For the multivector construction with nnn features and kkk folders,

(k−1)(n−1)≤Ndim(HΨ)≤kn.(k - 1)(n - 1) \le \mathrm{Ndim}(\mathcal H_\Psi) \le kn.(k−1)(n−1)≤Ndim(HΨ​)≤kn.

In plain words: the Natarajan dimension of one-weight-vector-per-folder is about the number of weights. For your filter, between 299×29=8,671299 \times 29 = 8{,}671299×29=8,671 and 9,0009{,}0009,000.

Proof. The upper bound is the theorem with d=knd = knd=kn. For the lower bound we shatter (k−1)(n−1)(k-1)(n-1)(k−1)(n−1) messages explicitly. Use the message x(i,j)\mathbf x(i, j)x(i,j), for i∈[k−1]i \in [k-1]i∈[k−1] and j∈[n−1]j \in [n-1]j∈[n−1], with a 1 in feature jjj, the number iii in the last feature, and zeros elsewhere. Candidates: f0=if_0 = if0​=i and f1=i+1f_1 = i + 1f1​=i+1.

Fix a column jjj and look at the scores of the messages x(1,j),…,x(k−1,j)\mathbf x(1, j), \dots, \mathbf x(k-1, j)x(1,j),…,x(k−1,j). Folder yyy scores x(i,j)\mathbf x(i, j)x(i,j) as wy,j+i wy,nw_{y,j} + i\, w_{y,n}wy,j​+iwy,n​: a straight line in iii, with intercept ay=wy,ja_y = w_{y,j}ay​=wy,j​ and slope wy,nw_{y,n}wy,n​. Set every slope to wy,n=yw_{y,n} = ywy,n​=y, shared by all columns. Lines yyy and y+1y + 1y+1 cross where ay+iy=ay+1+i(y+1)a_y + iy = a_{y+1} + i(y+1)ay​+iy=ay+1​+i(y+1), at i=ay−ay+1i = a_y - a_{y+1}i=ay​−ay+1​; call that crossing sys_ysy​. For i<syi < s_yi<sy​ line yyy is strictly higher, for i>syi > s_yi>sy​ line y+1y + 1y+1 is. Now choose, for each iii, si=i+0.4s_i = i + 0.4si​=i+0.4 if the mixture wants folder iii at x(i,j)\mathbf x(i, j)x(i,j), and si=i−0.4s_i = i - 0.4si​=i−0.4 if it wants i+1i + 1i+1; then set a1=0a_1 = 0a1​=0 and ay+1=ay−sya_{y+1} = a_y - s_yay+1​=ay​−sy​. The crossings increase strictly, si≤i+0.4<i+0.6≤si+1s_i \le i + 0.4 < i + 0.6 \le s_{i+1}si​≤i+0.4<i+0.6≤si+1​.

Take the message x(i,j)\mathbf x(i, j)x(i,j) and suppose the mixture wants folder iii, so i<sii < s_ii<si​; also si−1≤i−0.6<is_{i-1} \le i - 0.6 < isi−1​≤i−0.6<i. Comparing neighbours, line iii beats i+1i + 1i+1 (as i<sii < s_ii<si​), which beats i+2i + 2i+2 (as i<si+1i < s_{i+1}i<si+1​), and so on up; and line iii beats i−1i - 1i−1 (as i>si−1i > s_{i-1}i>si−1​), which beats i−2i - 2i−2, and so on down. All strictly, so folder iii wins with no tie. The case where the mixture wants i+1i + 1i+1 is the same argument with si<i<si+1s_i < i < s_{i+1}si​<i<si+1​. Each column’s intercepts are chosen independently, through the entries wy,jw_{y,j}wy,j​, so every mixture over all (k−1)(n−1)(k-1)(n-1)(k−1)(n−1) messages is achieved. ■\blacksquare■

Python builds the weights for every one of the 262^626 mixtures with k=4k = 4k=4 folders and n=3n = 3n=3 features, and checks that each message lands in the wanted folder with no tie:

from itertools import product

k, n = 4, 3
pts = [(i, j) for i in range(1, k) for j in range(1, n)]

def x(i, j):
    return [int(c == j) for c in range(1, n)] + [i]

def realize(want):
    w = {y: [0.0] * (n - 1) + [y] for y in range(1, k + 1)}
    for (i, j), label in want.items():
        t = i + 0.4 if label == i else i - 0.4
        w[i + 1][j - 1] = w[i][j - 1] - t
    return w

ok = 0
for B in product([0, 1], repeat=len(pts)):
    want = {p: p[0] + b for p, b in zip(pts, B)}
    w = realize(dict(sorted(want.items())))
    s = {p: [sum(a * b for a, b in zip(w[y], x(*p)))
             for y in range(1, k + 1)] for p in pts}
    ok += all(s[p].index(max(s[p])) + 1 == want[p]
              and s[p].count(max(s[p])) == 1 for p in pts)
print(len(pts), ok, 2 ** len(pts))

It prints 6 64 64: six messages, all 64 mixtures achieved.

So your 300-folder filter has Natarajan dimension between 8,671 and 9,000, and the multiclass fundamental theorem gives the review its answer, in the shape of the numbers printed earlier. One bug down.

Good and bad ERMs

Now the hungry folder. Let’s build the auto-folder class carefully, because it hides a surprise that the two-label world never showed us.

The domain X\mathcal XX is the set of senders (each message is filed by its sender), finite or even infinite. A user’s folder is a group of senders AAA. If X\mathcal XX is infinite we allow only groups that are finite or cofinite: either AAA is finite or everything outside AAA is. Write Pf(X)\mathcal P_f(\mathcal X)Pf​(X) for the collection of such groups (with a finite X\mathcal XX, every group qualifies). The labels are the groups themselves, together with one special label ∗\ast∗, “inbox”. For each group AAA, the rule

hA(x)={Aif x∈A,∗if x∉A,h_A(x) = \begin{cases} A & \text{if } x \in A, \\ \ast & \text{if } x \notin A, \end{cases}hA​(x)={A∗​if x∈A,if x∈/A,​

files mail from senders in AAA into the folder named AAA, and everything else into the inbox. The class is Hauto={hA:A∈Pf(X)}\mathcal H_{\mathrm{auto}} = \{h_A : A \in \mathcal P_f(\mathcal X)\}Hauto​={hA​:A∈Pf​(X)}. The big brace picks one of two lines depending on the condition on the right. In plain words: each rule names a group of senders, files their mail under that group’s name, and leaves the rest in the inbox. With A={Ana,Bo}A = \{\text{Ana}, \text{Bo}\}A={Ana,Bo}, mail from Bo goes to the folder “{Ana,Bo}\{\text{Ana}, \text{Bo}\}{Ana,Bo}” and mail from Cy to the inbox. The rule h∅h_\emptyseth∅​, with the empty group ∅\emptyset∅, keeps everything in the inbox.

With 1,000 senders there are 210002^{1000}21000 groups, so the folder count kkk is astronomical: 21000−12^{1000} - 121000−1 nonempty group names plus the inbox, 210002^{1000}21000 labels in all. And yet the class is tiny in the Natarajan sense.

Proposition. If X\mathcal XX has at least one sender, Ndim(Hauto)=1\mathrm{Ndim}(\mathcal H_{\mathrm{auto}}) = 1Ndim(Hauto​)=1.

Proof. One sender xxx is shattered with candidates {x}\{x\}{x} and ∗\ast∗: h{x}h_{\{x\}}h{x}​ and h∅h_\emptyseth∅​. Now suppose two senders x1,x2x_1, x_2x1​,x2​ were shattered. Every rule gives each sender either the inbox or the name of its own group, and a rule that names a group at both senders names the same group at both. At least one candidate at x1x_1x1​ is a group name, say AAA (the two candidates differ, so they are not both ∗\ast∗). Likewise x2x_2x2​ has a group-name candidate A′A'A′. The mixture choosing AAA at x1x_1x1​ and A′A'A′ at x2x_2x2​ needs a rule naming two groups at once, so A=A′A = A'A=A′, and the rule is hAh_AhA​ with both senders in AAA. But then the mixture choosing AAA at x1x_1x1​ and the other candidate at x2x_2x2​ needs a rule naming AAA at x1x_1x1​, which must be hAh_AhA​, and hAh_AhA​ gives x2x_2x2​ the label AAA too, not the other candidate. No rule achieves it, so no two senders are shattered. ■\blacksquare■

A brute-force check with four senders and all 16 groups:

from itertools import combinations as comb, product

n = 4
groups = [frozenset(g) for r in range(1, n + 1)
          for g in comb(range(n), r)] + [frozenset()]
H = [tuple(A if x in A else "*" for x in range(n))
     for A in groups]
labels = list(groups[:-1]) + ["*"]

def shatters(C):
    H_C = {tuple(h[x] for x in C) for h in H}
    return any(all(tuple(p[b] for p, b in zip(fs, B)) in H_C
                   for B in product((0, 1), repeat=len(C)))
               for fs in product(comb(labels, 2), repeat=len(C)))

sizes = [r for r in (1, 2)
         if any(shatters(C) for C in comb(range(n), r))]
print(len(H), len(labels), sizes)

It prints 16 16 [1]: 16 rules, 16 labels in use, and the only shattered size among 1 and 2 is 1.

### Every ERM, almost

Suppose the true rule is hAh_AhA​, and the training sequence SSS contains a message labelled with a group name. The only group name any rule can output for it is its own, so that name must be AAA, and only hAh_AhA​ outputs it. Any ERM must return a hypothesis with empirical risk 0, and hAh_AhA​ is the only one that fits that example: so every ERM returns the truth, with true risk 0. The ERMs can differ only on training sequences where every label is ∗\ast∗, all inbox:

S=((x1,∗),…,(xm,∗)).S = \big( (x_1, \ast), \dots, (x_m, \ast) \big).S=((x1​,∗),…,(xm​,∗)).

There, any hBh_BhB​ whose group BBB avoids every training sender is consistent. Two choices stand out.

  • Agood(S)=h∅A_{\mathrm{good}}(S) = h_\emptysetAgood​(S)=h∅​: when in doubt, keep everything in the inbox.
  • Abad(S)=h{x1,…,xm}cA_{\mathrm{bad}}(S) = h_{\{x_1, \dots, x_m\}^c}Abad​(S)=h{x1​,…,xm​}c​: make a folder out of every sender not seen. Here {x1,…,xm}c\{x_1, \dots, x_m\}^c{x1​,…,xm​}c is the complement of the seen senders, everyone else. It is cofinite, so the rule is in the class, and it is consistent because every training sender is outside it.

Both are ERMs: on sequences containing a group name both return hAh_AhA​, and on all-inbox sequences both return a consistent rule. Your team shipped AbadA_{\mathrm{bad}}Abad​.

Claim (the good ERM). Let ε,δ∈(0,1)\varepsilon, \delta \in (0, 1)ε,δ∈(0,1), let D\mathcal DD be any distribution over senders, and let the truth be any hA∈Hautoh_A \in \mathcal H_{\mathrm{auto}}hA​∈Hauto​. If

m≥log⁡(1/δ)ε,m \ge \frac{\log(1/\delta)}{\varepsilon},m≥εlog(1/δ)​,

then with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ over S∼DmS \sim \mathcal D^mS∼Dm, LD(Agood(S))≤εL_{\mathcal D}(A_{\mathrm{good}}(S)) \le \varepsilonLD​(Agood​(S))≤ε.

Read it: log⁡(1/δ)\log(1/\delta)log(1/δ) is the log of one over the failure chance, divided by the tolerance; no kkk, no number of senders, no dimension appears. S∼DmS \sim \mathcal D^mS∼Dm means the mmm senders are drawn independently from D\mathcal DD. In plain words: the good ERM needs only about log⁡(1/δ)/ε\log(1/\delta)/\varepsilonlog(1/δ)/ε labels, whatever the senders and folders. At ε=δ=0.05\varepsilon = \delta = 0.05ε=δ=0.05 that is log⁡20/0.05≈59.9\log 20/0.05 \approx 59.9log20/0.05≈59.9, so 60 labels.

Proof. AgoodA_{\mathrm{good}}Agood​ returns either hAh_AhA​ (true risk 0) or h∅h_\emptyseth∅​. It returns h∅h_\emptyseth∅​ only when no training sender is in AAA, and h∅h_\emptyseth∅​ errs exactly on mail from senders in AAA, so LD(h∅)=D(A)L_{\mathcal D}(h_\emptyset) = \mathcal D(A)LD​(h∅​)=D(A), the chance that a message comes from AAA. So a failure needs two things: D(A)>ε\mathcal D(A) > \varepsilonD(A)>ε, and all mmm independent draws land outside AAA. If D(A)≤ε\mathcal D(A) \le \varepsilonD(A)≤ε, failure is impossible. Otherwise each draw lands outside AAA with probability 1−D(A)<1−ε1 - \mathcal D(A) < 1 - \varepsilon1−D(A)<1−ε, and by independence all mmm do so with probability less than (1−ε)m(1 - \varepsilon)^m(1−ε)m. Finally, 1−ε≤e−ε1 - \varepsilon \le e^{-\varepsilon}1−ε≤e−ε (the line 1−u1 - u1−u lies below the curve e−ue^{-u}e−u, which it touches at u=0u = 0u=0), so

(1−ε)m≤e−εm≤e−log⁡(1/δ)=δ,(1 - \varepsilon)^m \le e^{-\varepsilon m} \le e^{-\log(1/\delta)} = \delta,(1−ε)m≤e−εm≤e−log(1/δ)=δ,

where the middle step uses m≥log⁡(1/δ)/εm \ge \log(1/\delta)/\varepsilonm≥log(1/δ)/ε. ■\blacksquare■

The worst case puts exactly ε\varepsilonε of the mail on the true group. Simulating it at ε=δ=0.05\varepsilon = \delta = 0.05ε=δ=0.05:

import random
from math import ceil, exp, log

eps, delta = 0.05, 0.05
m = ceil(log(1 / delta) / eps)
rng, trials = random.Random(0), 100_000
fails = sum(all(rng.random() >= eps for _ in range(m))
            for _ in range(trials))
print(m, round((1 - eps) ** m, 4), round(exp(-eps * m), 4),
      round(fails / trials, 4))

It prints 60 0.0461 0.0498 0.046: with 60 labels the exact failure chance (0.95)60(0.95)^{60}(0.95)60 is 4.6%, the bound e−3e^{-3}e−3 is 5.0%, and 100,000 simulated training sequences fail 4.6% of the time, under δ=5%\delta = 5\%δ=5%.

Claim (the bad ERM). Let X={x0,x1,…,xn−1}\mathcal X = \{x_0, x_1, \dots, x_{n-1}\}X={x0​,x1​,…,xn−1​} have n≥2n \ge 2n≥2 senders and let 0<ε≤1/20 < \varepsilon \le 1/20<ε≤1/2. Give the first sender most of the mail and spread the rest evenly:

D(x0)=1−2ε,D(xi)=2εn−1  for 1≤i≤n−1,\mathcal D(x_0) = 1 - 2\varepsilon, \qquad \mathcal D(x_i) = \frac{2\varepsilon}{n - 1} \ \text{ for } 1 \le i \le n - 1,D(x0​)=1−2ε,D(xi​)=n−12ε​  for 1≤i≤n−1,

and let the truth be h∅h_\emptyseth∅​. Then for every m≤(n−1)/2m \le (n-1)/2m≤(n−1)/2, and in particular every m≤(n−1)/6m \le (n-1)/6m≤(n−1)/6, every training sequence of size mmm leads AbadA_{\mathrm{bad}}Abad​ to a true risk of at least ε\varepsilonε. With m≤(n−1)/6m \le (n-1)/6m≤(n−1)/6 it is at least 5ε/35\varepsilon/35ε/3.

D(xi)\mathcal D(x_i)D(xi​) is the share of mail from sender xix_ixi​; the shares add to (1−2ε)+(n−1)⋅2ε/(n−1)=1(1 - 2\varepsilon) + (n-1) \cdot 2\varepsilon/(n-1) = 1(1−2ε)+(n−1)⋅2ε/(n−1)=1. In plain words: when most mail comes from one sender and the rest is spread thin, the bad ERM fails on every training sequence shorter than about half the number of senders. With n=1,000n = 1{,}000n=1,000 and ε=0.05\varepsilon = 0.05ε=0.05, that is the all-staff sender with 90% of the mail and 999 senders at 0.01% each, the opening’s simulation.

Proof. With the truth h∅h_\emptyseth∅​, every label is ∗\ast∗, so AbadA_{\mathrm{bad}}Abad​ returns the folder of all unseen senders and errs on every message from an unseen sender. At most mmm of x1,…,xn−1x_1, \dots, x_{n-1}x1​,…,xn−1​ can appear in mmm examples, so at least n−1−mn - 1 - mn−1−m of them are unseen, and

LD(Abad(S))≥(n−1−m)2εn−1=2ε−2εmn−1.L_{\mathcal D}(A_{\mathrm{bad}}(S)) \ge (n - 1 - m)\frac{2\varepsilon}{n - 1} = 2\varepsilon - \frac{2\varepsilon m}{n-1}.LD​(Abad​(S))≥(n−1−m)n−12ε​=2ε−n−12εm​.

With m≤(n−1)/2m \le (n-1)/2m≤(n−1)/2 the right side is at least ε\varepsilonε; with m≤(n−1)/6m \le (n-1)/6m≤(n−1)/6 it is at least 2ε−ε/3=5ε/32\varepsilon - \varepsilon/3 = 5\varepsilon/32ε−ε/3=5ε/3. This holds for every training sequence, so with probability 1. ■\blacksquare■

Here it is with 1,000 senders, ε=0.05\varepsilon = 0.05ε=0.05 and m=166m = 166m=166, the largest whole number below 999/6999/6999/6, over 2,000 random training sequences:

import random

n, eps = 1000, 0.05
p = [1 - 2 * eps] + [2 * eps / (n - 1)] * (n - 1)
m_max = (n - 1) // 6
rng, worst = random.Random(0), 1.0
for _ in range(2000):
    seen = set(rng.choices(range(n), weights=p, k=m_max))
    L_bad = sum(p[x] for x in range(n) if x not in seen)
    worst = min(worst, L_bad)
print(m_max, round(worst, 4), round(5 * eps / 3, 4))

It prints 166 0.0969 0.0833: the best the bad ERM ever did was a true risk of 9.7%, above the proven floor of 8.3% and far above ε=5%\varepsilon = 5\%ε=5%. The good ERM needed 60 labels; the bad one fails with 166, and with more senders it fails with more. Its sample complexity grows with the number of senders, while the good ERM’s does not depend on it at all.
