### What the hungry folder teaches

Three lessons hide in those two claims, and they are worth slowing down for.

Different ERMs can need wildly different numbers of labels. In the two-label world this never happens: the fundamental theorem makes every ERM a learner with the same rate. With many labels, the choice of tie-breaking is part of the learner, and it can cost you a factor of the number of senders.

Learnable does not mean learnable by every ERM. Let X\mathcal XX be infinite, say all possible email addresses. The good ERM still learns with ⌈log⁡(1/δ)/ε⌉\lceil \log(1/\delta)/\varepsilon \rceil⌈log(1/δ)/ε⌉ labels (the brackets round up), so the class is PAC learnable. But for any mmm, pick nnn senders with (n−1)/6≥m(n-1)/6 \ge m(n−1)/6≥m and the distribution of the bad-ERM claim on them: the bad ERM fails on every training sequence of size mmm. So no number of labels makes it a learner. And this rules out uniform convergence too: by lesson 4, uniform convergence would make every ERM a learner. So here is a class that is learnable, by a perfectly natural ERM, and yet has no uniform convergence property. For two labels, lesson 6b proved that impossible: learnability, uniform convergence and “every ERM learns” were one property. With many labels they come apart, and they come apart even with the plain 0-1 loss.

The log⁡k\log klogk in the theorem is not a ghost. The auto-folder class has Natarajan dimension 1, but with nnn senders it uses k=2nk = 2^nk=2n labels, so log⁡k=nlog⁡2\log k = n\log 2logk=nlog2. The theorem’s realizable ceiling, C2(dlog⁡(kd/ε)+log⁡(1/δ))/εC_2(d\log(kd/\varepsilon) + \log(1/\delta))/\varepsilonC2​(dlog(kd/ε)+log(1/δ))/ε, grows with nnn, and the bad ERM really does need on the order of nnn labels. And with infinitely many senders the label set is infinite, log⁡k=∞\log k = \inftylogk=∞, and the theorem says nothing, which is just as well, since the class lacks uniform convergence. The theorem covers every ERM, so it must pay for the worst one.

Can one always find a good ERM that avoids the log⁡k\log klogk? It has been conjectured that yes: that every class H⊆[k]X\mathcal H \subseteq [k]^{\mathcal X}H⊆[k]X has realizable sample complexity

mH(ε,δ)=O~ ⁣(Ndim(H)ε),m_{\mathcal H}(\varepsilon, \delta) = \tilde O\!\left( \frac{\mathrm{Ndim}(\mathcal H)}{\varepsilon} \right),mH​(ε,δ)=O~(εNdim(H)​),

where O~\tilde OO~ (“soft O”) means “at most a constant times this, up to factors that are powers of logarithms of 1/ε1/\varepsilon1/ε, 1/δ1/\delta1/δ and Ndim(H)\mathrm{Ndim}(\mathcal H)Ndim(H)”, and, crucially, no factor of kkk at all. In plain words: some learner should need only about the Natarajan dimension over the tolerance, however many folders there are. For the auto-folder class that is about 1/ε1/\varepsilon1/ε labels up to logs, and the good ERM’s 60 labels at ε=δ=0.05\varepsilon = \delta = 0.05ε=δ=0.05 fit it. This lesson leaves it as an open question.

### Certificates for the auto-folder filter

Back to the launch. You want a label budget backed by a proof, with numbers and no unknown constants. Two proofs are available.

The first covers every ERM at once. With nnn senders the class is finite, so lesson 2’s finite-class guarantee applies: in the realizable case, every ERM has true risk at most ε\varepsilonε with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ once m≥log⁡(∣H∣/δ)/εm \ge \log(|\mathcal H|/\delta)/\varepsilonm≥log(∣H∣/δ)/ε. Natarajan’s lemma bounds ∣H∣|\mathcal H|∣H∣ by the dimension, so

m≥dlog⁡n+2dlog⁡k+log⁡(1/δ)εm \ge \frac{d \log n + 2d \log k + \log(1/\delta)}{\varepsilon}m≥εdlogn+2dlogk+log(1/δ)​

certifies every ERM. Inside out: dlog⁡n+2dlog⁡kd\log n + 2d\log kdlogn+2dlogk is the log of Natarajan’s ndk2dn^d k^{2d}ndk2d, log⁡(1/δ)\log(1/\delta)log(1/δ) the price of confidence, and the division by ε\varepsilonε the realizable rate. In plain words: Natarajan’s count, put into the finite-class guarantee, certifies any ERM at all. The second proof covers only the good ERM, at log⁡(1/δ)/ε\log(1/\delta)/\varepsilonlog(1/δ)/ε. Here are both, for 1,000 senders, d=1d = 1d=1, ε=δ=0.05\varepsilon = \delta = 0.05ε=δ=0.05, along with the finite-class guarantee using the exact count ∣H∣=21000|\mathcal H| = 2^{1000}∣H∣=21000:

from math import ceil, log

n, d, eps, delta = 1000, 1, 0.05, 0.05
log_k = n * log(2)
natarajan = d * log(n) + 2 * d * log_k
every_erm = ceil((natarajan + log(1 / delta)) / eps)
direct = ceil((n * log(2) + log(1 / delta)) / eps)
good = ceil(log(1 / delta) / eps)
print(round(natarajan, 1), every_erm, direct, good)

It prints 1393.2 27924 13923 60. The log of Natarajan’s count is 1,393.2, so certifying every ERM costs 27,924 labels (13,923 with the exact count); certifying the good ERM costs 60. The difference is the price of not choosing your ERM.

The algorithms as code

Two algorithms came out of this lesson: computing the Natarajan dimension of a finite class by brute force, and the two ERMs for auto-folders.

Shatters(H, C, labels):
  H_C ← { (h(x) for x in C) : h in H }
  for each choice of one unordered pair {a_x, b_x}
        of labels per message x in C:
    if every B ⊆ C has (a_x if x in B else b_x)_x in H_C:
      return true
  return false

Ndim(H, X, labels):
  d ← 0
  for r = 1, 2, ..., |X|:
    if no C ⊆ X with |C| = r has Shatters(H, C, labels):
      return d
    d ← r
  return d

GoodERM(S):
  if some (x, y) in S has y ≠ *: return h_y
  return h_∅

BadERM(S):
  if some (x, y) in S has y ≠ *: return h_y
  return h_A with A = senders not in S

Stopping at the first size with no shattered set is safe: a subset of a shattered set is shattered with the same candidates, so if no set of size rrr is shattered, none larger is either.

Cost of Shatters. Building HC\mathcal H_CHC​ takes O(∣H∣ r)O(|\mathcal H|\, r)O(∣H∣r) time and space for a set of rrr messages (hashing tuples of length rrr). With kkk labels there are (k2)\binom{k}{2}(2k​) unordered pairs per message, so (k2)r\binom{k}{2}^r(2k​)r candidate choices, each checked against 2r2^r2r mixtures at O(r)O(r)O(r) per lookup: O(∣H∣ r+(k2)r2rr)O(|\mathcal H|\, r + \binom{k}{2}^r 2^r r)O(∣H∣r+(2k​)r2rr) time in the worst case. Ndim calls it for every set of each size up to d+1d + 1d+1: ∑r≤d+1(nr)\sum_{r \le d+1} \binom{n}{r}∑r≤d+1​(rn​) sets, exponential in ddd. That is fine for the tiny classes of this lesson and hopeless for your 300-folder filter, which is why the bounds of the previous section matter: for real classes we compute the dimension by proof, not by search.

Cost of the ERMs. Both scan SSS once, O(m)O(m)O(m) time. GoodERM stores nothing beyond the answer; BadERM stores the set of seen senders, O(m)O(m)O(m) space, and its returned rule is described by that set. Same cost, same training error, very different futures.

Build it yourself. Using only the Python standard library:

from itertools import combinations, product

def levels(n, k):
    return [h for h in product(range(1, k + 1), repeat=n)
            if list(h) == sorted(h)]

def auto_folders(n):
    groups = [frozenset(g) for r in range(n + 1)
              for g in combinations(range(n), r)]
    return [tuple(A if x in A else "*" for x in range(n))
            for A in groups]

def shatters(H, C, labels): ...
def ndim(H, n, labels): ...
def good_erm(S, n): ...
def bad_erm(S, n): ...

if __name__ == "__main__":
    assert shatters(levels(3, 3), (0, 2), [1, 2, 3])
    assert not shatters(levels(3, 3), (0, 1, 2), [1, 2, 3])
    assert ndim(levels(5, 3), 5, [1, 2, 3]) == 2
    assert ndim(levels(5, 2), 5, [1, 2]) == 1
    H = auto_folders(4)
    labels = sorted({v for h in H for v in h}, key=str)
    assert ndim(H, 4, labels) == 1
    A = frozenset({1, 3})
    S = [(0, "*"), (2, "*"), (0, "*")]
    assert good_erm(S, 4) == ("*",) * 4
    assert bad_erm(S, 4) == ("*", A, "*", A)
    assert good_erm(S + [(3, A)], 4) == ("*", A, "*", A)
    assert bad_erm(S + [(3, A)], 4) == ("*", A, "*", A)
    print("ok")
  1. Implement shatters, ndim (labels passed explicitly), good_erm and bad_erm. A hypothesis is a tuple of labels, one per message; a group label is a frozenset; "*" is the inbox. The ERMs return the rule as a tuple over senders 0..n-1.
  2. Reproduce the Natarajan dimensions 1, 2, 3 of urgency levels with two, three and four folders, and 1 for auto-folders on four senders.
  3. Simulate both ERMs with 1,000 senders and the distribution of the bad-ERM claim at ε=0.05\varepsilon = 0.05ε=0.05, for m=60,166,500,2,000m = 60, 166, 500, 2{,}000m=60,166,500,2,000. At what mmm does the bad ERM first reach true risk ε\varepsilonε? Compare with (n−1)/2(n-1)/2(n−1)/2.
  4. Build one-versus-all over thresholds for k=3k = 3k=3 on seven scores and compute its Natarajan dimension. Is it kdkdkd?

Fix the bug

Two bugs, two fixes. The review gets its answer from the multiclass fundamental theorem: your 300-folder filter has Natarajan dimension between 8,671 and 9,000, so its sample complexity is sandwiched between constant multiples of the shapes printed earlier, with log⁡300\log 300log300 between floor and ceiling.

The auto-folder filter is yours to fix in the lab. There are 1,000 senders, the all-staff sender sends 90% of the mail, and your users have a budget of 120 labels. You must hit ε=δ=0.05\varepsilon = \delta = 0.05ε=δ=0.05, and not by luck: you have to pick a label budget and an ERM whose true risk this lesson has proved is at most ε\varepsilonε with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ. First you will compute the Natarajan dimension of the auto-folder class, because the every-ERM certificate needs it. Then choose your ERM and your budget, and watch the folders.

[lab-act2: built on the lesson page]

What people get wrong

“With kkk labels, shattering means producing all k∣C∣k^{|C|}k∣C∣ filings.” That is far too strict: urgency levels never achieve “high score, low folder”, yet they are a perfectly learnable class. Shattering asks only for every mixture of two candidates per message, candidates you choose.

“More folders means proportionally more labels.” The number of folders enters the theorem only through log⁡k\log klogk, and for a good ERM perhaps not at all. Going from 300 folders to 3,000 multiplies log⁡k\log klogk by about 1.4.

“Any ERM will do.” For two labels, yes, and that is lesson 6a’s theorem. With many labels, two ERMs with the same training error can differ by a factor of the number of senders in the labels they need, and with infinitely many labels one can learn while the other never does.

“If a class is learnable, it has uniform convergence.” The auto-folder class with infinitely many senders is learnable, by the good ERM, and has no uniform convergence property. The equivalence was a two-label fact.

Recap and the next bug

  1. With many labels, a set CCC is shattered when you can choose two different candidate folders for each message so that the class achieves every mixture of them. The Natarajan dimension is the size of the largest shattered set; with two labels it is the VC dimension.
  2. Natarajan’s lemma: a class of Natarajan dimension ddd on nnn messages has at most ndk2dn^d k^{2d}ndk2d members, playing the role Sauer’s lemma played.
  3. The multiclass fundamental theorem: finite Natarajan dimension ddd (with finitely many labels kkk) means learnable, with sample complexity between constant multiples of (d+log⁡(1/δ))/ε2(d + \log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon^2(d+log(1/δ))/ε2 and (dlog⁡k+log⁡(1/δ))/ε2(d\log k + \log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon^2(dlogk+log(1/δ))/ε2 in the agnostic case, and similar shapes over ε\varepsilonε in the realizable case.
  4. Calculations: one-versus-all and every reduction with lll filters of VC dimension ddd have Natarajan dimension at most 3ldlog⁡(ld)3ld\log(ld)3ldlog(ld); linear multiclass predictors in Rd\mathbb R^dRd at most ddd; the multivector construction between (k−1)(n−1)(k-1)(n-1)(k−1)(n−1) and knknkn. Roughly, the number of parameters.
  5. Good and bad ERMs: for auto-folders, keeping everything in the inbox learns with log⁡(1/δ)/ε\log(1/\delta)/\varepsilonlog(1/δ)/ε labels, while foldering the unseen senders needs labels in proportion to the number of senders; with infinitely many senders the class is learnable but has no uniform convergence.

The filter is certified, and the auto-folders behave. Then the auditor from compliance stops by with a question you didn’t expect. She has been reading the archive of old filters, and she noticed something about the tightest-box filter, the one that draws the smallest axis-aligned rectangle around the junk examples. “You told me the box is learned from all your labelled messages,” she says. “But I can rebuild it from just four of them: the leftmost, rightmost, highest and lowest junk messages. The other examples don’t matter at all.” Then she asks: if a rule can be compressed to a handful of its own training examples, does that alone guarantee that it generalizes, with no VC dimension anywhere in sight? That is the next lesson.
